fields.title: The Key Teachings of John Bunyan
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of John Bunyan’s message — the burden and the cross, the Slough of Despond, Doubting Castle and the key called Promise, the river and the Celestial City — and the discovery that set him free: that a believer’s righteousness is not in his own heart but in heaven, in Jesus Christ Himself. Twenty short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as a companion to Bunyan’s own public-domain works, which readers are warmly encouraged to go to directly.
fields.about_html:
This is not a book by John Bunyan. It is a companion to him — an independent work of exposition and appreciation, written by Ochorus, that follows the pilgrim’s road of The Pilgrim’s Progress and the soul-history of Grace Abounding through twenty short chapters for the ordinary reader, with a chapter on his life, a conclusion and a guide to his books.

Bunyan’s one theme was the journey of a sinner to God, and the one Person who makes it possible. The road runs from the City of Destruction by the wicket gate and the cross, up the Hill Difficulty and down into the valleys, through Vanity Fair and out of Doubting Castle, to the river and the city beyond; and everything on it depends on Christ, whose righteousness, as the tinker of Elstow discovered in a field outside Bedford, is kept safe in heaven whatever the pilgrim feels. This volume walks that road, weighs honestly the places where Bunyan must be read with care — the allegory is not Scripture, his own extreme religious anxiety calls for gentle handling, and the Second Part reflects its century’s view of women — and ends each chapter in a few questions and a prayer.

Bunyan’s own writings are in the public domain and freely available, and every chapter here names them so the reader can go to the source; The Pilgrim’s Progress and Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners are both in the Ochorus library. This companion is offered only to open the door. It quotes Scripture from the Authorised (King James) Version, and it makes no claim to stand in for the plain, searching pages of the man himself.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul. 1 PETER 2:11

John Bunyan was a tinker, a mender of pots and kettles, from a village just south of Bedford. He had a little reading and writing and no other learning. He never went to university, never held a living in the Church of England, and spent twelve of his best years in the county gaol for preaching without a licence. And yet the book he began in that gaol has been read, for more than three hundred years, by more people in more languages than almost any book but the Bible. For generations of English-speaking households there were two books on the shelf: the Bible, and The Pilgrim’s Progress.

A man who had been there

The reason is not that Bunyan was clever, though he was, nor that he could tell a story, though he could tell one better than almost anyone in his century. The reason is that every mile of the road he described he had walked himself. The burden on Christian’s back was the weight he had carried through years of terror. The Slough of Despond was mud he had sunk in. Doubting Castle was a prison he had lain in long before the magistrates put him in theirs. When the burden rolls away at the cross, it rolls away because Bunyan’s own chains had fallen off in a field outside Bedford. He wrote in the preface to his autobiography that God did not play in convincing him, nor the devil in tempting him, and so he could not play in telling it. That is the secret of his power. He is plain because he is serious.

One road, and one Person on it

The thread that runs through everything Bunyan wrote is this: the Christian life is a journey, and the only way through it is Christ. It is a journey — not a single moment, not a settled estate, but a road with a beginning and an end, with gates and hills and valleys, with enemies and friends, with wrong turnings and hard climbs. Bunyan never pretended that the road was easy. And the whole of it depends on Christ — Christ at the cross, where the burden falls; Christ at God’s right hand, where the believer’s righteousness is kept safe; Christ at the river, where the pilgrim at last feels the bottom and finds it good.

Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. JOHN 14:6

How this book is arranged

After a chapter on his life, twenty short chapters set out his teaching. Sixteen of them follow the pilgrim’s road through the First Part of The Pilgrim’s Progress, from the burden and the book to the river and the Celestial City. Then three chapters turn to Grace Abounding and to Bunyan’s own soul: the temptation to sell Christ, the sentence that set him free, and the preacher in Bedford gaol. A last teaching chapter follows Christiana and her company in the Second Part, where Bunyan gathers up the weak and the fearful and brings them home.

Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. Bunyan would not have wanted his dream admired and left on the shelf. At the close of the First Part he turns to the reader and bids him interpret the dream to himself. Read a chapter a day, or one a week. Stop at the application points. Pray the prayer, or better, pray your own. And keep his books open beside this one; they are far better than any account of them.

Where he must be read with care

This is not a book of hero-worship, and it is better to say plainly at the start where Bunyan must be weighed rather than simply received.

First, The Pilgrim’s Progress is an allegory, not Scripture. It is a picture of the Christian life, drawn by a godly and gifted man, and it is full of Scripture — his margins are crowded with references. But a picture is not a doctrine, and not every detail of the dream is meant to be pressed. Some believers never pass through a Slough of Despond; some lose their burden in a different order from Christian. Bunyan knew this; the Second Part itself shows pilgrims travelling the same road very differently. Use the dream as a mirror and a map, never as a rule that God must follow in your life.

Second, Bunyan’s own soul-history includes years of extreme religious anxiety. Grace Abounding records blasphemous thoughts he could not stop, the terror that he had committed the unpardonable sin, and long seasons in which every verse he read seemed to condemn him. Many readers have found in it the comfort of company in the dark. But readers who are themselves prone to scrupulous fear, to obsessive doubts about their salvation, should read those chapters gently — perhaps with a wise friend or pastor — and should notice above all how Bunyan came out: not by finding a better feeling in himself but by looking away from himself to Christ. Chapters nineteen and twenty take particular care here.

Third, the Second Part of The Pilgrim’s Progress is a book of its time in its view of women. Christiana and Mercy are among the most lovely figures Bunyan drew, and the Second Part honours women’s faith warmly. But the women are guarded and guided by men as a matter of course, and some of his remarks reflect seventeenth-century assumptions rather than anything Scripture requires. He should be read as the man he was.

Why read him, then? Because on the central matter he was right. We are strangers and pilgrims. The road is narrow and the burden is real, but there is a place, somewhat ascending, where it falls from the back and is seen no more. The counsel of this book is the counsel of Scripture: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Where Bunyan is faithful — on sin and grace, on the cross, on perseverance, on the sufficiency of Christ — receive it gladly. Where the dream says more than the Bible, enjoy the story and let the Bible decide.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before going further, ask yourself honestly where you are on the road: still in the City of Destruction, struggling towards the gate, or somewhere along the way.

2. Choose a pace for this book, and decide now whether you will read The Pilgrim’s Progress alongside it. If you have never read it through, begin this week.

3. Write down one experience in your own life — a hard season, a deliverance — that you have never thought of as part of your journey with God.

4. If you are prone to anxious fears about your salvation, decide now to read the chapters on Bunyan’s temptations with a trusted friend, and to keep your eyes on Christ rather than on your feelings.

5. Resolve to test everything in these pages, and in Bunyan’s, against Scripture.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are the way, and there is no other. I thank You for Your servant John Bunyan, who walked the road before me and drew it so plainly.
As I read of his burden, his fears and his deliverances, show me my own. Where I am off the road, call me back; where I am weary, strengthen me; where I am afraid, let me see You.
Keep me from admiring a dream and missing the Saviour at its heart. Let every page send me to Your cross and to Your Word.
And bring me at the last, with all Your pilgrims, safe over the river and home. Amen.

fields.title: The Tinker of Elstow
fields.body_html:
This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief. 1 TIMOTHY 1:15

A tinker’s son. John Bunyan was born in 1628 at Harrowden, a hamlet in the parish of Elstow, a mile or so south of Bedford, and was baptised in Elstow church on 30 November that year. His father, Thomas, was a tinker, a mender of pots and kettles, and John followed him into the trade. The family were poor, though they owned their cottage. Bunyan later described his father’s house as among the meanest in the land, with that mixture of humility and bluntness that runs through all his writing. He was taught to read and write, and then, as he tells it, set himself to forget whatever good he had learned.

A lad of the village. Grace Abounding is merciless about his youth. He swore, he lied, he broke the Sabbath, he was the ringleader of the young men of Elstow in their games and mischief. Readers looking for a great scandal behind the self-accusation generally fail to find one. His sins were the ordinary sins of an ordinary young man, seen through a conscience that God later gave eyes.

The soldier. In 1644 his mother died, and within weeks his sister; his father married again almost at once. That same year, at about sixteen, Bunyan was mustered into the Parliamentary army in the Civil War and served in the garrison at Newport Pagnell. He saw little fighting. But he remembered all his life that at one siege another man asked to go in his place, and was shot in the head as he stood sentinel. Bunyan counted it a mercy, and admitted that at the time it did not move him at all.

Two books and a dish and a spoon. After the army he came home, took up the tinker’s trade and married. History has not kept his first wife’s name. They were, he says, as poor as poor might be, without so much as a dish or a spoon between them. But she brought with her two books that had belonged to her godly father, Arthur Dent’s The Plain Man’s Pathway to Heaven and Lewis Bayly’s The Practice of Piety, and they read them together. The books did not convert him, but they began something. He went to church twice a day, admired the priest and the vestments, and became outwardly very religious. Their first child, Mary, was born in 1650. She was blind, and she lay, he said, nearer his heart than all the rest.

A voice on the green. One Sunday, in the middle of a game of cat — a village stick-and-ball game, as he was about to strike the second blow, a question darted into his soul: would he leave his sins and go to heaven, or keep his sins and go to hell? He looked up to heaven and seemed to see the Lord looking down on him, displeased. He concluded, in despair, that it was too late for him, and went back to his game. Not long after, a woman of the village, no saint herself, rebuked him for his cursing outside her shop window, and to his own amazement he gave up swearing. He reformed his life and was pleased with himself. He was, by his own account, a brisk talker in religion.

Poor women in the sun. Then, about 1651, his work took him into Bedford, and in one of its streets he came upon three or four poor women sitting at a door in the sun and talking about the things of God. He drew near, expecting to join in. He could not. He heard, but he did not understand. They spoke of a new birth, of the work of God on their hearts, of the promises that held them up under temptation, and of their own righteousness as worthless. They seemed to him to have found a new world. He went back to them again and again, and they told their pastor, John Gifford, about him. Gifford, a former Royalist officer who had himself been converted out of a wild life, took the tinker in, invited him to his house and taught him. Bunyan joined the little Bedford congregation in 1653.

The years in the dark. What followed was not peace but the long ordeal told in chapters nineteen and twenty: years of doubt and temptation, ended at last by a sentence that fell on his soul in a field.

The tinker in the pulpit. The Bedford church soon saw that their tinker could preach. About 1655 the brethren asked him to speak, first privately and then in the villages round about. Crowds came to hear him, and he preached, as he said, what he felt. He also began to write, first in controversy with the Quakers in Some Gospel Truths Opened, then in a stream of books that never stopped. His first wife died about 1658, leaving him with four young children, and in 1659 he married Elizabeth, a young woman of the congregation.

Arrest. In 1660 Charles II came back to the throne, and with him the laws against worship outside the Church of England. In November that year Bunyan went to preach at a farmhouse at Lower Samsell, near Harlington. He was warned that a warrant was out for him. He would not run, lest his flight should discourage the weak. The constable came in as the meeting began. At the next sessions he was indicted for upholding unlawful meetings and for refusing to attend the parish church. The justices required only that he promise to stop preaching. He would not promise. He stayed in Bedford gaol, with a few brief intervals, for twelve years.

Elizabeth before the judges. Elizabeth was expecting a child when he was taken. The shock brought on labour, and the baby died. In 1661 she went three times to plead for her husband, the last time before Sir Matthew Hale and his fellow judges at the Bedford assizes, telling them that she had four small children, one of them blind, and nothing to live on but the charity of good people. Hale was moved, but said he could do nothing. She went home with nothing.

The prison years. The gaol was not a dungeon; Bunyan had visitors, and for a time some liberty. He made long tagged laces to support his family, and he wrote: Christian Behaviour, The Holy City, I Will Pray with the Spirit, and in 1666 Grace Abounding.

The dream in the den. Somewhere in these years, perhaps near the end of the long imprisonment or during a shorter one later, Bunyan began to write an allegory, almost as a diversion from graver work. It opens with a man walking through the wilderness of this world, lying down in a den and dreaming. The den was the gaol. The Pilgrim’s Progress was published in 1678 and sold at once. A Second Part, following Christian’s wife Christiana and her children, came out some years later.

Bishop Bunyan. In 1672, under the King’s Declaration of Indulgence, Bunyan was released and licensed to preach, and the Bedford congregation, which had already chosen him as its pastor, received him home. For sixteen years he preached, visited the scattered meetings of the county, travelled to London where great crowds came to hear him, and wrote — among much else The Life and Death of Mr Badman and The Holy War. Friends and enemies alike nicknamed him Bishop Bunyan. He was imprisoned again for some months in the mid-1670s.

The last journey. In August 1688 he rode to Reading to reconcile a father and a son who had quarrelled, and succeeded. Riding on to London through heavy rain, he arrived soaked at the house of his friend John Strudwick on Snow Hill, and fell ill with a fever. He died there on 31 August 1688, aged fifty-nine, and was buried in Bunhill Fields, the burial ground of the Dissenters. His last errand had been to make peace.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Bunyan’s turning came through a wife’s two books, a voice on the green, some poor women talking in the sun and a patient pastor. List the ordinary people and means God used to reach you, and thank Him for each by name.

2. The women at the door spoke of things Bunyan did not understand. Ask whether your conversation about God is the kind that would make a religious talker hungry for more.

3. Bunyan would not promise to stop preaching, and it cost his family dearly. Is there any faithfulness God is asking of you that will cost you something? Count the cost honestly.

4. Pray this week for someone imprisoned for their faith today.

5. His last journey was to reconcile a father and son. Is there a quarrel you could help to mend?

A PRAYER
Lord, You found John Bunyan on a village green and in a Bedford street, and You would not let him go.
Thank You for the people and the books, the voices and the providences, by which You have found me.
Give me the courage he had to be faithful when faithfulness is costly, and the tenderness he had for those I love.
And make me, like him at the last, a maker of peace. Amen.

fields.body_html:
For mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me. PSALM 38:4

The Pilgrim’s Progress does not begin with a sunrise or a birth or a call. It begins with a man in rags, standing with his face turned from his own house, a book in his hand and a great burden on his back. As he reads, he weeps and trembles, and at last he breaks out with a cry: “What shall I do?” That is the first picture Bunyan gives us of the Christian life, and it is not a flattering one. Before a man is a pilgrim, he is a man in trouble.

The weight no one else could see

The burden is the first great image of the book, and Bunyan’s margin tells us what it means. It is sin — not a feeling of unease, not a vague dissatisfaction with life, but the guilt of a real person before a real God. The man has read in his book that his city will be burned with fire from heaven, and that he himself is condemned to die and after that to come to judgement. He is not willing to do the first, he tells Evangelist, nor able to do the second.

And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment. HEBREWS 9:27

What is striking is how lonely the burden is. The man goes home and tries to hide his distress from his wife and children. When he can bear it no longer and tells them, they think some frenzy has got into his head and put him to bed, hoping sleep will settle his brains. The next day they are harsh with him; then they deride him; then they neglect him. He goes out alone into the fields to read and pray.

The book in his hand

Notice what has done this to him. It is not a sermon, not a vision, not a disaster. It is the book. The man has been reading, and the more he reads the heavier the burden grows. Bunyan never needed to explain which book he meant. The margins of The Pilgrim’s Progress are thick with references, and Christian answers every argument on the road by saying, in effect, read it in my book.

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. HEBREWS 4:12

What shall I do to be saved

Walking in the fields, reading as he was wont, the man bursts out again, crying, “What shall I do to be saved?” It is the jailer’s question at Philippi, and Bunyan puts the reference in the margin. He looks this way and that, as if he would run, but he stands still, because he cannot tell which way to go.

And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house. ACTS 16:30–31

That picture of a man wanting to run and not knowing where is exactly right. Conviction on its own does not save anyone. It only makes a person restless. Bunyan knew that the devil is quite content for a soul to be troubled so long as it stays still — so long as it goes on feeling bad about sin without ever getting to Christ. The burden is meant to drive us somewhere. That is why the next person on the road is Evangelist.

Fly from the wrath to come

Evangelist gives the man a parchment roll, and written within are the words, “Fly from the wrath to come.” The man asks where to fly, and Evangelist points him over a wide field to a wicket gate he cannot yet see, and a shining light he thinks he can. Then the man begins to run.

O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come? MATTHEW 3:7

Here is the most famous and the most troubling moment in the opening pages. As he runs, his wife and children see him and cry after him to return. But the man puts his fingers in his ears and runs on crying, “Life! life! eternal life!” He does not look behind him.

Readers have sometimes been shocked by this, and it needs careful handling. Bunyan puts two texts in the margin: the words of Christ that no one can be His disciple who does not hate father and mother, wife and children, and the angel’s warning to Lot not to look back. He is not commending the abandonment of a family. Everything we know of Bunyan the husband and father — his agony in gaol over his blind daughter, his tenderness towards Elizabeth — tells against that. He is drawing, in the bold lines of a dream, the truth that nothing, not even the dearest human love, may hold a soul back from Christ. And the story does not end here. Christian pleads with his family before he leaves, and the whole Second Part of the book is the story of how his wife and children followed him.

If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple. LUKE 14:26

Obstinate and Pliable

Two neighbours come after the man to fetch him back — for now we learn his name is Christian. Obstinate will not hear a word; he lumps Christian among the crazy-headed coxcombs who are wiser in their own eyes than seven men that can render a reason, tells Pliable to come home, and goes home himself. Pliable is more promising. He listens eagerly as Christian describes the endless kingdom, the crowns of glory, the company of the holy, and the place where all tears will be wiped away. Glad to hear of such things, he urges that they mend their pace. Christian answers that he cannot go as fast as he would, because of the burden on his back.

But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it; yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while. MATTHEW 13:20–21

1. Have you ever felt the burden of your sin before God — not just regret, but guilt? If not, ask God this week to show you yourself as He sees you.

2. Christian’s burden came from reading his book. Read Romans 3:9–26 slowly and let it do its work.

3. If you are carrying something heavy that those around you cannot see, tell one trusted believer about it.

4. Examine yourself for the marks of Pliable: an attraction to heaven with no grief over sin. Where is your faith all promise and no repentance?

5. If you have prayed for years for family who mock or ignore your faith, take heart from the Second Part: Christiana came at last. Keep praying.

Keep me from a religion that wants heaven without repentance; give me a true sense of my need and a true sight of Christ.
And for those I love who do not yet see, have mercy, and bring them after me on the road. Amen.

fields.title: The Slough of Despond
fields.body_html:
He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings. PSALM 40:2

Christian and Pliable have not gone far when, talking of crowns and glory and heedless of their feet, they fall suddenly into a bog in the middle of the plain. Its name is Despond. They wallow in the dirt, and Christian, because of the burden on his back, begins to sink. Pliable, offended, asks whether this is the happiness he was promised, struggles out on the side nearest his own house and goes home. Christian is left to tumble in the Slough alone.

What the Slough is

Bunyan does not leave us to guess. As the dreamer watches, a man named Help draws Christian out, and the dreamer asks why this place has never been mended, so that poor travellers might pass more safely. Help explains that it cannot be mended. It is the low ground into which the scum and filth that attend conviction for sin continually run. As a sinner is awakened to his lost condition, there arise in his soul many fears and doubts and discouraging apprehensions, and they all settle here. That is why the ground is so bad.

So the Slough is not ordinary sadness, nor even depression, though it can feel like both. It is the particular despondency of a newly awakened conscience. A person begins to see his sin, and at once a flood of fears pours in: that it is too late, that he has sinned too much, that God will not receive him, that he is not really sincere. Bunyan had spent years in that mud. He knew exactly what it smelled like.

Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul. I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me. PSALM 69:1–2

Why Christian sinks and Pliable does not

There is a sharp observation hidden here. Both men fall in, but only Christian sinks, and he sinks because of his burden. Pliable has no burden. He is muddy and offended, but in no danger, and he climbs out easily — on the wrong side. Christian, weighed down by the sense of his sin, cannot get out at all, but he struggles towards the side farthest from his own house and nearest the gate.

That is a picture every pastor recognises. The person who feels most deeply the weight of sin is often the one most tempted to despair; the one who feels it least is the one who gives up most easily. Despondency is not a sign that you are not a true pilgrim. It may be a sign that you are. What matters is which side of the Slough you are struggling towards.

The steps that were there all along

Help asks Christian a simple question: why did you not look for the steps? For, as he later tells the dreamer, there are good and substantial steps placed through the very middle of the Slough, by the direction of the Lawgiver. In Bunyan’s original margin the steps are the promises of forgiveness and acceptance by faith in Christ. But when the weather turns and the Slough spews out its filth, the steps are hard to see, and men through dizziness step beside them and are bemired, though the steps are there.

Christian’s answer is honest: fear followed him so hard that he fled the nearest way and fell in. That is how most of us fall into despondency. We do not calmly weigh the promises of God and reject them. We panic. Fear chases us, and we run the nearest way, and the steps that would have held us are right there under the muddy water.

Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath: that by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us. HEBREWS 6:17–18

Grace Abounding is in large part the story of a man learning to find the steps. Bunyan tells how, in his worst agonies, he would flounce towards a promise as a horse stuck in the mire flounces towards sound ground. He did not always feel it holding him. But he learned that the promise was there whether he felt it or not, and that the business of a despondent soul is to put its foot on the word of God and stand.

Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. JOHN 6:37

Help

The other great comfort of the Slough is the man called Help. He comes to Christian, asks him plainly what he is doing there, gives him his hand, draws him out, sets him on sound ground and bids him go on his way. Bunyan puts Psalm 40 in the margin. Help is the Lord’s own hand reaching into the pit — but in the story He reaches through a person.

Many of us have been pulled out of the Slough by someone. Bunyan was: by the poor women of Bedford, by John Gifford, by the fellowship of a small congregation that took a troubled tinker seriously. Help does not lecture. He asks one question, gives one hand and sends Christian on. There is a whole ministry in that. If you are in the mire, look for Help; do not be too proud to take a hand. If you are on firm ground, be Help to someone else.

Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness. GALATIANS 6:1

The Slough that cannot be mended

Perhaps the most honest thing Bunyan says here is that the Slough cannot be mended. The King’s labourers have worked on it for sixteen hundred years; millions of cartloads of wholesome instruction have been thrown into it; and it is the Slough of Despond still. In the Second Part, when Christiana comes this way, she hears that it is even worse, because many who pretend to be the King’s labourers bring dirt and dung instead of stones, and so mar instead of mending.

A caution for the scrupulous

Bunyan’s picture is true, but it is not a law. Not every believer passes through a long Slough; some go over the steps dry-shod. And those who are prone to anxiety or depression should not conclude that their darkness must be spiritual, or that a true Christian will not struggle with low spirits. Some despondency is conviction; some is illness, grief or exhaustion, and needs a doctor or a friend as much as a sermon. The steps are still there in every case. But do not load a heavy heart with the extra fear that its heaviness proves it is lost.

The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit. PSALM 34:18
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Have you ever been in the Slough — overwhelmed with fears and doubts after seeing your sin? Which side were you struggling towards?

2. Write out three promises of God that are, for you, steps through the mire. Keep them where you will see them when fear chases you.

3. Think of someone who was Help to you. Thank God for them, and if you can, thank them.

4. Is there someone near you sinking in discouragement? Offer a hand this week: one question, one kindness, one word of Scripture.

5. If your low spirits have lasted long, consider whether you need a doctor or a counsellor as well as a pastor, and do not be ashamed to seek help.

A PRAYER
Lord, when fear has chased me into the mire, and my sins have weighed me down, You have not left me there.
Show me the steps You have laid through the Slough — Your promises, sure and substantial, whether I see them or not — and give me courage to stand on them.
Thank You for every Help You have sent me. Make me a help to others who are sinking.
And set my feet upon a rock, and establish my goings, until I stand on the good ground within the gate. Amen.

fields.title: Mr Worldly Wiseman and the Hill
fields.body_html:
Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ. GALATIANS 2:16

Out of the Slough and walking alone, Christian meets a gentleman crossing the field. His name is Mr Worldly Wiseman, and he lives in the town of Carnal Policy, a very great town not far from the City of Destruction. He has heard of Christian’s setting out, for it has become the talk of the neighbourhood, and he sees at once the dirt of the Slough upon him. He is kindly, reasonable and full of good sense. He is also the most dangerous man Christian has yet met.

Sensible counsel

Worldly Wiseman does not mock the burden, as Obstinate did. He takes it seriously. Get rid of it with all speed, he says; you will never be settled in your mind till then. But the way Evangelist has sent you is the most dangerous and troublesome way in the world. Look at you already — the Slough is only the beginning. Ahead lie weariness, pain, hunger, perils, nakedness, sword, lions, dragons, darkness and death. Why should a man throw himself away by listening to a stranger?

Then he offers a better way. Flashes of fire come out of the hill. He stands still, sweating and trembling, and does not know what to do.

3. Read Galatians 3:10–14 and 3:21–26. Write in one sentence what the law can do and what it cannot.

fields.title: The Wicket Gate
fields.body_html:
Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it. MATTHEW 7:13–14

At last, after the Slough and the hill, Christian comes to the gate. Over it is written, “Knock, and it shall be opened unto you.” He knocks, more than once or twice, and while he waits he makes a little rhyme, asking whether the one within will open to him, though he has been an undeserving rebel. It is the prayer of every sinner who has ever stood at the door of mercy wondering if it will open.

A small gate at the way’s head

Bunyan calls it a wicket gate: a small door set in or beside a larger gate, just wide enough for one person at a time. Evangelist had pointed to it across a very wide field, and Christian could not at first see it. That is right. The entrance to the Christian life is small and easily missed. There is no grand portal and no crowd. One person comes, one at a time, and knocks.

The gate stands, in Bunyan’s dream, at the head of the way. Everything before it — the burden, the Slough, the hill — is conviction and struggle. Everything after it is the pilgrim’s road. Bunyan uses the gate for that decisive moment when an awakened sinner comes to Christ Himself, and is received. The burden will not fall until later, at the cross; but the pilgrim is on the road now, and the road is Christ’s.

I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture. JOHN 10:9

I am willing with all my heart

A grave person comes to the gate, whose name is Goodwill. He asks who is there. Christian answers, in effect, a poor burdened sinner from the City of Destruction, going to Mount Zion to be delivered from the wrath to come, and asks if he is willing to let him in. And Goodwill replies, “I am willing with all my heart,” and opens the gate.

If there is one sentence in the whole book to carry home, it may be that one. Bunyan had spent years believing that Christ was unwilling — that He might receive other sinners but not one who had done what Bunyan had done. The discovery that set him free was that the Lord is willing, with all His heart. Goodwill is not reluctant or grudging. He does not examine Christian’s record before opening. He opens, and then asks.

And, behold, there came a leper and worshipped him, saying, Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean. And Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean. MATTHEW 8:2–3

Arrows at the gate

Then something strange happens. As Christian steps in, Goodwill gives him a pull. Christian asks what that means, and Goodwill explains that a little distance from the gate stands a strong castle of which Beelzebub is captain, and from it he and his company shoot arrows at those who come up to the gate, hoping they may die before they can enter in. Christian answers, “I rejoice and tremble.”

This is Bunyan the experienced pastor speaking. He knew that the moments when a soul is nearest to Christ are the moments of fiercest attack. Grace Abounding is full of it: just when he began to hope, a new temptation would come; just when a promise began to warm him, a terrible text would fly at him. The devil does not trouble much about those who are content in the City of Destruction. He shoots at those at the gate. So if you have found that coming to Christ has stirred up more fear, more doubt and more temptation than you had before, do not conclude you are on the wrong road. You are being shot at because you are near the door.

My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: and I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. JOHN 10:27–28

In no wise cast out

Once inside, Christian confesses how he turned aside to Mr Worldly Wiseman and almost perished under the hill, and says he hardly deserves to be let in. Goodwill’s answer is one of the loveliest things in the book: “We make no objections against any, notwithstanding all that they have done before they come hither; they in no wise are cast out.” The margin gives John 6:37.

That verse was, perhaps more than any other, the anchor of Bunyan’s soul. In Grace Abounding he tells how it visited him in the worst of his troubles: “Oh, the comfort that I have had from this word, ‘in no wise’!” He explains that it means by no means, for no thing, whatever a man has done. Satan laboured to pull the promise from him, telling him that Christ meant other sinners of a lower rank; but Bunyan answered that there was no such exception in the words. Some years later he wrote a whole treatise on the verse, Come and Welcome to Jesus Christ, and it remains one of the warmest invitations to sinners in the English language.

All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. JOHN 6:37

The narrow way

Goodwill then shows Christian the way he must go. It was cast up by the patriarchs, prophets, Christ and His apostles, and it is, in his words, “as strait as a rule can make it.” Christian asks whether there are no turnings by which a stranger might lose his way. Goodwill answers that there are many ways butting down on this one, and they are crooked and wide; but the right may be known from the wrong because only the right is straight and narrow.

Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. JEREMIAH 6:16

The burden not yet gone

Christian then asks Goodwill to help him off with his burden. Goodwill tells him to be content to bear it until he comes to the place of deliverance, for there it will fall from his back of itself.

Theologians have argued over this detail. Does Bunyan mean that a person can enter by the gate — come to Christ — and still carry guilt? The best answer is that he is describing experience, not the legal fact. Every believer who comes to Christ is justified at once. But many do not feel the full release at once. Bunyan had not. He had joined the Bedford church and walked with its people for some time before his chains fell off in the field. The dream is honest about that gap. If you have come to the gate and still feel the burden, do not turn back. Keep walking towards the cross.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Have you knocked at the gate — come personally to Christ, not merely to church or to religion? If not, knock today.

2. Memorise John 6:37. Say the words “in no wise” slowly, and apply them to the worst thing you have done.

3. If coming close to Christ has stirred up fresh fear or temptation, name it as an arrow from the castle, and take refuge inside the gate.

4. Think of one person who believes they are too bad to be received. How could you tell them about Goodwill?

5. Ask where you are tempted to leave the narrow way for a wider, more comfortable one.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are the door, and You are willing with all Your heart. I have stood outside too long, fearing that You would not open.
I come as a poor burdened sinner. Receive me, for You have said that You will in no wise cast out anyone who comes.
When the arrows fly at me, pull me in and hold me fast. When I am tempted to think my sin too great, remind me of Your word.
And set my feet on the narrow way, and keep me on it until I come to the place of deliverance. Amen.

fields.title: The Interpreter’s House
fields.body_html:
But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you. JOHN 14:26

Beyond the gate, Christian comes to the house of the Interpreter, knocks over and over, and is let in. The Interpreter lights a candle and leads him from room to room, showing him a series of pictures and scenes, and explaining each one. It is the schoolroom of The Pilgrim’s Progress. The pilgrim has entered the way; now he must learn to understand it.

Bunyan never says in so many words who the Interpreter is, but the reader of Scripture has little doubt. It is the Holy Spirit, who takes the things of Christ and shows them to us. The Interpreter does not add new revelations. He opens what is already there, so that a new believer can see it. And that is the first lesson of the house: the Christian life cannot be lived on first impressions. We need to be taught.

The picture of the true guide

The first thing the Interpreter shows Christian is a picture of a very grave person. It has eyes lifted up to heaven, the best of books in its hand, the law of truth written on its lips, the world behind its back. It stands as if it pleaded with men, and a crown of gold hangs over its head. This, the Interpreter explains, is the only kind of man whom the Lord of the country has authorised to be Christian’s guide in all difficult places; he shows it first, so that Christian may not be misled by those who pretend to lead him right but whose way goes down to death.

It is Bunyan’s portrait of a faithful minister, and it is worth pausing on, for he spent his life trying to be one. The true guide looks to God, holds to Scripture, speaks the truth, has turned his back on worldly reward, and pleads with people for their souls. Bunyan does not care whether he is learned, ordained by a bishop or eloquent. He cares whether he has these marks. It is a searching test for preachers, and a useful one for anyone choosing whom to listen to.

Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation. HEBREWS 13:7

The dusty parlour

Next the Interpreter leads Christian into a large parlour full of dust, never swept. He calls a man to sweep it, and at once the dust flies about so thickly that Christian is almost choked. Then the Interpreter bids a damsel bring water and sprinkle the room, and it is swept and cleansed with pleasure.

The parlour, the Interpreter says, is the heart of a man never sanctified by the sweet grace of the gospel. The dust is original sin and inward corruption. In a little room sit two children. Passion is discontented; Patience is quiet. Their governor would have them wait for their best things till the next year, but Passion will have all now. And then he adds a wonderful thought: Passion had less reason to laugh at Patience for having his good things first than Patience will have to laugh at Passion for having his best things last. The Interpreter then shows Christian a fire burning against a wall, and a man continually casting water on it to quench it; yet the fire burns higher and hotter. Round the back of the wall stands another man, secretly pouring oil into the fire from a vessel.

Make me resolute to enter, and keep me from the cage of despair. Amen.

fields.title: The Burden Loosed at the Cross
fields.body_html:
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed. 1 PETER 2:24

If you know one scene from The Pilgrim’s Progress, it is probably this one. It takes up barely half a page. Bunyan tells it with such plainness that a child can follow it, and yet it has comforted theologians and dying saints for three centuries. It is the still centre of the whole book.

Up the way called Salvation

Leaving the Interpreter’s house, Christian comes into a highway fenced on either side by a wall, and the wall is called Salvation. Up this way he runs, but not without great difficulty, because of the load on his back. He runs until he comes to a place somewhat ascending, and on that place stands a cross, and a little below, in the bottom, a sepulchre.

We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks. ISAIAH 26:1

The burden falls of itself

Just as Christian comes up with the cross, his burden loosens from his shoulders, falls from his back, and begins to tumble, and goes on tumbling until it comes to the mouth of the sepulchre, where it falls in, and the dreamer sees it no more.

Every word counts. Christian does not untie the burden. He does not throw it off. He does not even pray for it to be removed at that moment. He comes to the cross, and it falls. Goodwill had told him, back at the gate, that it would fall from his back of itself at the place of deliverance, and so it does. The relief of guilt is not something we achieve by effort. It is something that happens when we come to Christ crucified.

Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. ISAIAH 53:4–5

And it goes into the sepulchre — into the tomb of Christ — and is seen no more. The burden is not merely set down by the road where Christian might pick it up again. It is buried. The dreamer looks for it and cannot find it.

As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us. PSALM 103:12

Rest by His sorrow, life by His death

Christian’s first words are among the most beautiful Bunyan ever wrote: “He hath given me rest by his sorrow, and life by his death.” In a single sentence he has the whole doctrine of the atonement. Christ’s sorrow is my rest; Christ’s death is my life. There is an exchange at the heart of the gospel, and Christian feels it before he can explain it.

Then he stands still a while to look and wonder, for it is very surprising to him that the sight of the cross should thus ease him of his burden. He looks, and looks again, until the tears run down his cheeks. Bunyan puts Zechariah 12:10 in the margin: they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him.

And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him. ZECHARIAH 12:10

That is a lovely detail. The first response to forgiveness is not a theory but wonder, and the wonder is mixed with tears. Christian is glad and lightsome and merry of heart — and weeping. Joy and grief meet at the cross, as Bunyan says at the close of Grace Abounding: “of all joy, that is the sweetest that is mixed with mourning over Christ.”

The three Shining Ones

As Christian stands weeping, three Shining Ones come to him and greet him with, “Peace be to thee.” The first tells him that his sins are forgiven. The second strips off his rags and clothes him with a change of raiment. The third sets a mark on his forehead and gives him a roll with a seal on it, which he is to look on as he runs and to hand in at the celestial gate.

Bunyan has gathered here, in three simple gifts, the great blessings of the gospel. Forgiveness: the guilt is gone. New clothing: the filthy rags of his own righteousness are exchanged for the righteousness of Christ, as Joshua the high priest was stripped and clothed in Zechariah’s vision. The mark and the sealed roll: the seal of the Spirit and the assurance of acceptance, a certificate he can read on the road and present at the end.

Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. PSALM 32:1
In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise. EPHESIANS 1:13

Three leaps for joy

Then Christian gives three leaps for joy and goes on singing. His song asks what place this is, and whether this must be the beginning of his bliss, and blesses the cross, the sepulchre, and the Man who was put to shame for him.

The honest questions

There are two honest questions to set beside this scene.

First, why does the burden fall at the cross and not at the gate? Bunyan is describing experience, and his own experience was that assurance of forgiveness came some time after he had first come to Christ. Many believers are like that; many others are not, and find gate and cross in the same hour. The dream does not require a gap. What it requires is that the burden be lost at the cross and nowhere else — not at Legality’s house, not by sweeping the parlour.

Second, does the burden never come back? In the story it does not. But Christian will know fear, doubt and despair again; he will be beaten by Apollyon and imprisoned by Giant Despair. Bunyan knew that the guilt of sin, once buried in Christ’s tomb, is gone for ever, but that the feeling of assurance can come and go. The answer, when it goes, is always the same: go back to the cross and look again.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Isaiah 53 slowly, aloud if you can, and stand still a while to look and wonder.

2. Write out Christian’s sentence — rest by His sorrow, life by His death — and put your own name in it.

3. Is there a sin you keep digging up again after Christ has buried it? Confess it once more, and then leave it in the sepulchre.

4. Consider the three gifts: forgiveness, new clothing, the seal. Which do you most need to believe today?

5. Find a way this week to express joy in your salvation — a song, a psalm, a gift, a word of thanks to someone.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I came to Your cross with nothing but my burden, and You took it away. You gave me rest by Your sorrow and life by Your death.
Let me never grow used to that wonder. Let me look, and look again, until my heart is broken and glad together.
Clothe me in Your righteousness, seal me with Your Spirit, and let me read Your promise as I run.
And when my old guilt whispers again, bring me back to the cross and the empty tomb, where it was buried and is seen no more. Amen.

fields.title: The Hill Difficulty
fields.body_html:
Wherefore lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees; and make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed. HEBREWS 12:12–13

The burden has gone. Christian is clothed, sealed and singing. A reader might expect the rest of the book to be easy. Instead, within a page, Bunyan brings his pilgrim to the foot of a hill so steep that he falls from running to walking, and from walking to clambering on his hands and knees. The hill is called Difficulty.

Those who came over the wall

Before he reaches the hill, Christian meets two travellers who come tumbling over the wall on the left hand of the way. Their names are Formalist and Hypocrisy, born in the land of Vain-glory and going, for praise, to Mount Zion. Christian asks why they did not come in at the gate. They say that all their countrymen count the gate too far about, and that it is their custom to take a short cut over the wall — a custom, they add, of more than a thousand years’ standing. If we are in, we are in, they say; what matter how we got here?

Christian’s reply is sharp. He walks by the rule of his Master; they walk by the rude working of their fancies. They came in by themselves without His direction, and will go out by themselves without His mercy. When they sneer at his coat, he tells them it was given him by the Lord of the place, in the day He stripped him of his rags, and that he hopes to be known by it at the gate.

Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber. JOHN 10:1

Formalist and Hypocrisy stand for a religion of outward form without inward change — church-going, ceremonies, custom and respectability, with no burden, no gate and no cross. Bunyan, who had been hauled before magistrates for refusing the forms of the national church, had strong feelings about religion by custom. But the warning is not only for others. Any of us can come to rely on having been brought up in the way, rather than on having come in by the door.

The choice at the foot of the hill

At the bottom of the hill is a spring, and there two other paths branch off, one to the left and one to the right. The narrow way goes straight up. Christian drinks from the spring and begins to climb, singing a song that ends: “Better, though difficult, the right way to go” than the wrong way that is easy and ends in woe. Formalist and Hypocrisy, seeing how steep the hill is, suppose the easier paths will join the narrow way on the other side. One takes the way called Danger and is lost in a great wood; the other takes the way called Destruction and falls among dark mountains and rises no more.

Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able. LUKE 13:24

That is the whole lesson of the hill. The Christian life is not meant to be arranged for comfort. There will be places where obedience is simply hard: a sin to be given up, a wrong to be confessed, a costly duty to be done, a loss to be borne. At those places there will always be a path round, which promises to rejoin the way later. It never does.

The arbour and the lost roll

Halfway up is a pleasant arbour, made by the Lord of the hill for the refreshment of weary travellers. Christian sits down, pulls out his roll and reads it, and looks again at the coat given him at the cross. Pleasing himself a while, he falls into a slumber, then into a fast sleep, and sleeps until it is almost night. As he sleeps, the roll falls out of his hand. Someone wakes him with the words of Proverbs, “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise,” and he starts up and hurries on to the top.

Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. PROVERBS 6:6

Bunyan is careful here. The arbour is good; the Lord made it. Rest is not sin, and reading one’s assurance is not sin. The trouble begins with pleasing himself — resting not in Christ but in the enjoyment of his own privileges — and then in the rest becoming sleep. It is possible to be so taken up with the comfort of being forgiven that we stop climbing. And it is in that drowsy self-congratulation that assurance slips out of our hands.

Going back for it

At the top Christian meets two men running down, Timorous and Mistrust, who tell him there are lions ahead and they are going home. Christian is afraid, but reasons it through: to go back is nothing but death; to go forward is fear of death, and life everlasting beyond it. He will go forward. Then he feels in his bosom for his roll, to comfort himself, and finds it gone.

What follows is one of the most tender passages in the book. Christian falls on his knees and asks God’s forgiveness for his foolish sleep, then goes back down the hill, sighing, weeping, chiding himself, looking on this side and that for his roll. At the arbour he sits down and weeps, and at last, looking sorrowfully under the settle, he sees it. He catches it up with trembling and haste. For this roll, Bunyan says, was the assurance of his life and acceptance at the desired haven.

Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit. PSALM 51:12

The chained lions

fields.title: The Palace Beautiful
fields.body_html:
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God. EPHESIANS 2:19

At the top of the Hill Difficulty, past the chained lions, stands a very stately palace by the highway side. Its name is Beautiful. The porter tells Christian that it was built by the Lord of the hill for the relief and security of pilgrims. Here Christian is received, questioned, fed, rested, taught and armed, and sent on his way with friends walking beside him down the hill.

Almost every reader of Bunyan has understood the Palace Beautiful as a picture of the local church. Bunyan never says so outright, but the details make it plain, and it is worth remembering who drew it. Bunyan belonged all his adult life to a small gathered congregation in Bedford — the people who took him in when he was a troubled young tinker, who taught him, examined him, received him, and later chose him as their pastor while he lay in prison. The Palace Beautiful is his thank-offering to them.

Received after conversation

Christian does not simply walk in. The porter, Watchful, rings a bell and calls a grave and beautiful damsel named Discretion, who asks Christian where he is from, where he is going, how he got into the way and what he has met on it. Then she asks his name. When he answers, she smiles, but the water stands in her eyes, and she calls Prudence, Piety and Charity, who talk with him further and then bring him into the family. Many of the household meet him at the threshold and say: Come in, thou blessed of the Lord.

This reflects the practice of Bunyan’s own church, which received members by hearing their account of God’s dealings with their souls. Some modern readers find that intrusive. But notice the spirit of it. Discretion’s questions are not an interrogation. She wants to know the story, and when she hears it she weeps for joy. The church is not a club that admits anyone indifferently, nor a court that tries candidates. It is a household that rejoices to recognise a brother or a sister.

Bunyan also held, against many of his fellow Baptists, that disagreement over baptism should not bar believers from fellowship at the Lord’s Table, and he wrote more than one book on the point. His Palace receives pilgrims because they have come through the gate and by the cross, not because they belong to a party.

Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God. ROMANS 15:7

Piety, Prudence and Charity

Piety asks about the journey — what moved him to become a pilgrim, what he saw at the Interpreter’s house, what he saw at the cross. She is teaching him to remember and to testify. Christian says that the things he has told her were the best, and he means the cross.

Prudence asks about the inner life. Does he think of the country he came from? Does he still carry some of its thoughts with him? Christian answers honestly that he does, greatly against his will; when he would do the best, the worst is with him. Does he find those things sometimes vanquished? Yes, he says, but seldom, and those are golden hours to him. And how are they vanquished? Here Christian gives an answer worth learning by heart: “when I think what I saw at the cross, that will do it”; and so will looking at his coat, reading his roll, and letting his thoughts grow warm about where he is going.

For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not. ROMANS 7:18

This is Bunyan’s whole practical theology of holiness in a few lines. Indwelling sin remains. Victory is real but not constant. And the means of victory is not self-scrutiny but looking away from self: to the cross, to the righteousness given, to the promise held, to the glory ahead.

Charity asks about his family. Why did he not bring them? Christian weeps. He tried, he says; he talked to them, prayed for them, showed them his fears over and over; but his wife was afraid of losing this world and his children were given to the foolish delights of youth. Charity presses him: did his own vain life undo his words? Christian admits many failings, but says that if anything in him hindered them, it was his tenderness about sinning against God, for which they called him too precise.

Table, study and armoury

Supper follows, and all the talk at table is of the Lord of the hill: that He had been a great warrior, and had fought with and slain him that had the power of death, but not without great danger to Himself, and with the loss of much blood; and that He did it out of pure love. The church’s table-talk, in Bunyan’s dream, is Christ.

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil. HEBREWS 2:14

In the morning they show him the study, with its records of the Lord’s pedigree and acts, the deeds of His servants, and, above all, how willing their Lord is to receive into His favour any, even any, though they have offered Him great affronts in time past. The church is a place of memory and instruction, where the new believer learns the story he has joined.

Then they take him to the armoury, where the Lord has provided sword, shield, helmet, breastplate, all-prayer and shoes that will not wear out, enough to harness as many men as there are stars in the sky. They show him Moses’ rod, Jael’s hammer and nail, Gideon’s trumpets, Samson’s jawbone and David’s sling. From the roof they show him, far off, the Delectable Mountains. And before he leaves, they harness him from head to foot, lest he meet with assaults in the way.

Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. EPHESIANS 6:11

Sent out, not shut in

The last thing to notice about the Palace Beautiful is that Christian leaves it. He would gladly stay, and they would gladly keep him, but he has further to go. The church in Bunyan’s dream is not the destination; it is a house by the highway, built for the relief and security of pilgrims on their way. It feeds, rests, teaches and arms them, and then it walks with them to the gate and sends them on.

Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching. HEBREWS 10:25
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Are you a member of a local church, belonging to a household and not merely visiting? If not, what is holding you back?

2. Ask Prudence’s question of yourself: by what means do you find your sins vanquished? Is it by looking at the cross, or by looking at yourself?

3. Think of one new believer in your church. How could you be Discretion to them — asking to hear their story, and rejoicing in it?

4. Pray for anyone in your church grieving over family who will not come.

5. Examine the armoury of Ephesians 6:10–18. Which piece have you been leaving on the rack?

A PRAYER
Lord of the hill, thank You for the house You built by the highway for weary pilgrims, and for the people who took me in.
Make Your church in my day a Palace Beautiful: a place of welcome, of honest questions and tender answers, of table-talk about You.
When my sins trouble me, turn my eyes to what I saw at the cross. Arm me from head to foot for what lies ahead.
And let me be to others what Discretion, Piety, Prudence and Charity were to Christian, for Jesus’ sake. Amen.

fields.title: Apollyon in the Valley of Humiliation
fields.body_html:
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me. MICAH 7:8

The friends from the Palace Beautiful walk with Christian down the hill. Prudence warns him that it is a hard matter for a man to go down into the Valley of Humiliation and catch no slip by the way, and even with their help he catches a slip or two. At the bottom they give him bread, wine and raisins and send him on alone. He has gone only a little way when he sees a foul fiend coming over the field to meet him. His name is Apollyon.

A monster who argues

Apollyon is hideous: clothed in scales like a fish, with wings like a dragon, feet like a bear, fire and smoke coming out of his belly and a mouth like a lion’s. Christian’s first thought is to turn back. Then he remembers that his armour has no piece for his back. To run would only expose him. So he resolves to stand his ground.

Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. JAMES 4:7

Apollyon opens with a claim of ownership. Christian comes from the City of Destruction; therefore he is one of Apollyon’s subjects, for all that country is his. How dare he run from his king? Christian answers that he was indeed born in Apollyon’s dominions, but that the service was hard and the wages such as a man could not live on, for the wages of sin is death.

Then Apollyon tries bargaining. Come back, and I will give you what my country can afford. Christian replies that he has let himself to another, the King of princes. Apollyon tries sympathy: many of that King’s servants give Him the slip after a while; do the same, and all shall be well. Christian says he has sworn allegiance; how can he go back? Apollyon offers to forgive and forget. And Christian answers that what he promised Apollyon was in his nonage, and that the Prince under whose banner he now stands is able to absolve him even of that. Then he says, simply, that he likes his new Master’s service, wages, servants, government, company and country better. “I am his servant, and I will follow him.”

The accusation

Then comes the cruellest weapon. Apollyon accuses. You have already been unfaithful, he says. You fainted in the Slough. You tried wrong ways to be rid of your burden. You sinfully slept and lost your roll. You nearly turned back at the lions. And when you talk of your journey you are inwardly desirous of vainglory in all you say.

And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night. REVELATION 12:10

Every accusation is true. That is what makes it so deadly. And Christian’s answer is the answer every believer needs. He does not deny it. He says: all this is true, and much more that you have left out. But the Prince I serve is merciful and ready to forgive; I have groaned under these infirmities, been sorry for them, and obtained pardon of my Prince.

That is how Bunyan learned to fight the accuser. In Grace Abounding he describes long seasons in which Satan brought his sins before him, one after another, and he had no answer until he learned to say, in effect: yes, I am a great sinner, but Christ is a great Saviour. The accuser wins only when we argue about our record. He loses when we plead Christ’s.

Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. ROMANS 8:33–34

Half a day of fighting

Now Apollyon breaks into a rage. He straddles the whole breadth of the way, swears by his infernal den that Christian shall go no further, and throws a flaming dart at his breast. Christian catches it on his shield. Then the darts come thick as hail, and Christian is wounded in his head, his hand and his foot. The combat lasts above half a day, and Christian grows weaker and weaker.

At last Apollyon closes with him, wrestles him down, and Christian’s sword flies out of his hand. “I am sure of thee now,” says the fiend, and presses him almost to death. But as Apollyon fetches his last blow, Christian nimbly reaches out, catches his sword and cries the words of Micah: Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise. He gives Apollyon a deadly thrust, and then another, crying, Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors, through Him that loved us. And Apollyon spreads his dragon wings and flies away.

Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. ROMANS 8:37

The sword is the word of God, and Christian’s two thrusts are two verses of Scripture. Bunyan does not make him win by courage or skill, for he has almost none left. He wins by grasping the word when he is flat on his back. That, too, was Bunyan’s experience: again and again in Grace Abounding it is a single sentence of Scripture that turns the battle.

And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. EPHESIANS 6:17

Wounds and healing

The dreamer says that he never saw Christian give so much as one pleasant look all through the fight, until he saw he had wounded Apollyon; then he smiled and looked upward. Christian gives thanks, and a hand appears with leaves of the tree of life, which he applies to his wounds and is healed at once. He eats and drinks the bread and wine his friends gave him, and goes on with his sword drawn.

Why the Valley of Humiliation

Why does Apollyon meet Christian here, of all places? In the Second Part, when Christiana passes this way, Great-heart tells her that the Valley of Humiliation is in itself as fruitful a place as any the crow flies over, and that Christian’s trouble there came from his own slips on the way down. A pillar stands there warning those who come after to take heed of Christian’s slips before he came hither. Great-heart adds that our Lord formerly had His country-house in this valley and loved to walk its meadows, and they hear a shepherd boy singing that he that is down needs fear no fall.

That is a wonderful balance. Humiliation — the lowering of our pride — is a place where the devil fights hard, especially when we come into it carelessly, still proud of our privileges. But it is also the place Christ loved most, and where humble pilgrims find peace. The same valley is a battlefield for the proud and a meadow for the lowly.

He must increase, but I must decrease. JOHN 3:30
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Which of Apollyon’s arguments do you hear most often — ownership, bargaining, sympathy, threat or accusation? Write down your answer to it from Scripture.

2. When the accuser brings your sins before you, practise Christian’s reply: all this is true, and more; but my Prince is merciful, and I have obtained pardon.

3. Memorise Micah 7:8 and Romans 8:37 as weapons for the day when your sword has fallen out of your hand.

4. If you are wounded from a long fight, receive the healing God provides: rest, fellowship, the Lord’s Supper, His Word.

5. Ask God to make you lowly, so that the Valley of Humiliation may be for you a meadow and not only a battlefield.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I was born in the enemy’s country, but You have bought me, and I am Your servant. I like Your service, Your wages, Your people and Your country better than his.

When I am down and my sword has fallen, put Your Word back in my hand. When I fall, let me arise.

MICAH 7:8 The friends from the Palace Beautiful walk with Christian down the hill. Prudence warns him that it is a hard matter for a man to go down into the Valley of Humiliation and catch no slip by the way, and even with their help he catches a slip or two. At the bottom they give him bread, wine and raisins and send him on alone. He has gone only a little way when he sees a foul fiend coming over the field to meet him. His name is Apollyon. A monster who argues Apollyon is hideous: clothed in scales like a fish, with wings like a dragon, feet like a bear, fire and smoke coming out of his belly and a mouth like a lion’s. Christian’s first thought is to turn back. Then he remembers that his armour has no piece for his back. To run would only expose him. So he resolves to stand his ground. Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. JAMES 4:7 Apollyon opens with a claim of ownership. Christian comes from the City of Destruction; therefore he is one of Apollyon’s subjects, for all that country is his. How dare he run from his king? Christian answers that he was indeed born in Apollyon’s dominions, but that the service was hard and the wages such as a man could not live on, for the wages of sin is death. Then Apollyon tries bargaining. Come back, and I will give you what my country can afford. Christian replies that he has let himself to another, the King of princes. Apollyon tries sympathy: many of that King’s servants give Him the slip after a while; do the same, and all shall be well. Christian says he has sworn allegiance; how can he go back? Apollyon offers to forgive and forget. And Christian answers that what he promised Apollyon was in his nonage, and that the Prince under whose banner he now stands is able to absolve him even of that. Then he says, simply, that he likes his new Master’s service, wages, servants, government, company and country better. “I am his servant, and I will follow him.” The accusation Then comes the cruellest weapon. Apollyon accuses. You have already been unfaithful, he says. You fainted in the Slough. You tried wrong ways to be rid of your burden. You sinfully slept and lost your roll. You nearly turned back at the lions. And when you talk of your journey you are inwardly desirous of vainglory in all you say. When the accuser brings your sins before you, practise Christian’s reply: all this is true, and more; but my Prince is merciful, and I have obtained pardon. 3. Memorise Micah 7:8 and Romans 8:37 as weapons for the day when your sword has fallen out of your hand. 4.
