fields.title: The Valley of the Shadow of Death
fields.body_html:
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me. PSALM 23:4

Beyond the Valley of Humiliation lies another valley, and Christian must go through it, because the way to the Celestial City runs through the middle of it. At its edge he meets two men hurrying back. They tell him it is as dark as pitch, full of hobgoblins, satyrs and dragons of the pit, with a continual howling, and that death spreads his wings over it. Christian answers that by all they have said he perceives it is his way to the desired haven. Be it thy way, they reply; we will not choose it for ours.

Bunyan is not describing physical death here; that comes at the river. The Valley of the Shadow of Death is a spiritual darkness — a season in which the believer walks in blackness, surrounded by terrors, unable to see the way or to feel God near. Bunyan had walked there for years. It is the most personal place in the whole dream.

A narrow path between two dangers

The path through the valley is exceeding narrow. On the right is a very deep ditch, into which the blind have led the blind in all ages. On the left is a dangerous quag, into which, if even a good man falls, he finds no bottom; King David once fell into it and would have been smothered had not He that is able plucked him out. In the dark, when Christian tries to shun the ditch, he is ready to tip into the mire, and when he avoids the mire he nearly falls into the ditch. Often, when he lifts his foot, he does not know where he will set it next.

Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink: let me be delivered from them that hate me, and out of the deep waters. PSALM 69:14

All-prayer

About the middle of the valley is the mouth of hell, hard by the wayside. Flames, smoke and sparks come out of it, with hideous noises, and they care nothing for Christian’s sword. So he puts up his sword and takes another weapon, called All-prayer, and cries, O Lord, I beseech thee, deliver my soul. He goes on a great while, hearing doleful voices and rushings to and fro. Once he hears what he thinks is a company of fiends coming to meet him, stops, and half thinks to go back. Then he remembers how many dangers he has already come through, and resolves to go on, crying out that he will walk in the strength of the Lord God. The fiends give back and come no further.

Then called I upon the name of the LORD; O LORD, I beseech thee, deliver my soul. PSALM 116:4

There is deep wisdom in the change of weapons. Against Apollyon, who argued, Christian fought with the word. Against these terrors, which do not argue but simply overwhelm, argument is useless. There is nothing to answer, only something to endure. And for that the weapon is prayer — not eloquent prayer, but a cry. In the darkest seasons of the Christian life, the only prayer we may be able to pray is a single sentence, repeated for miles. It is enough.

The whispered blasphemies

Then comes a passage that Bunyan says he would not let slip, and it is one of the kindest things he ever wrote. When Christian comes over against the mouth of the burning pit, one of the wicked ones gets behind him, steps up softly, and whispers many grievous blasphemies to him, which Christian verily thinks have come from his own mind. This troubles him more than anything he has met before — to think that he should now blaspheme Him whom he loves so much. If he could have helped it, he would not have done it; but he has not the discretion either to stop his ears or to know where the blasphemies came from.

Bunyan is describing, from the inside, something that torments many sincere Christians: intrusive, unwanted, horrifying thoughts against God. Grace Abounding shows that he suffered exactly this. For months, blasphemous thoughts poured into his mind against his will, and he concluded that they proved he was lost. Here, years later, he tells his readers what he wished someone had told him. Those thoughts did not come from Christian’s heart. They were whispered by an enemy behind him. He hated them, and that hatred was the proof that they were not his.

Now then it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me. ROMANS 7:17

If you are troubled by such thoughts, this passage is for you. Unwanted thoughts that horrify you are not the unpardonable sin. They are not evidence that you do not love God; your distress at them is evidence that you do. Do not argue with them, and do not examine them endlessly to see whether you consented. Turn from them to Christ, and if they persist, tell a wise pastor or a doctor, for this kind of torment is well known and can be helped.

A voice ahead in the dark

When Christian has travelled in this disconsolate condition a considerable time, he hears the voice of a man going before him, saying, Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for thou art with me. He is glad, for three reasons. Others who fear God are in this valley too. God is with them in the dark, though they cannot perceive it — and why not, then, with him? And he hopes to overtake them and have company.

Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not: he passeth on also, but I perceive him not. JOB 9:11

The shadow of death turned to morning

By and by the day breaks, and Christian says, “He hath turned the shadow of death into the morning.” He looks back — not from any desire to return, but to see by daylight the hazards he came through in the dark. Now he sees the ditch, the quag, and how narrow the way was between them; he sees the hobgoblins and dragons, but all afar off.

Seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning. AMOS 5:8

Then Bunyan tells us something unexpected. The second part of the valley is far more dangerous than the first — full of snares, traps, gins and nets, pits and pitfalls. Had it been dark, Christian could not have survived it with a thousand souls. But just now the sun is rising, and he goes through by its light, saying with Job, His candle shineth on my head, and by his light I go through darkness.

At the end of the valley Christian passes the cave of two giants, Pope and Pagan, among the bones of martyred pilgrims. Pagan is long dead; Pope, grown old and stiff, sits grinning at pilgrims and biting his nails. This is the Protestant polemic of Bunyan’s century, written by a man who remembered the Marian burnings, and it should be read as such. Its lasting point is simpler: the persecutors of past ages, however terrible, could not stop the pilgrims, and their power passes away.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Have you walked through a Valley of the Shadow of Death — a season of spiritual darkness? What kept you on the narrow path?

2. If you are in the dark now, choose one short prayer, such as Psalm 116:4, and pray it whenever the terrors come.

3. If you are troubled by unwanted blasphemous or horrifying thoughts, remember that the whisperer is behind you. Tell one trusted person this week, and stop cross-examining yourself.

4. Be a voice ahead for someone else. Is there a believer you know in the dark to whom you could say plainly, I have been here too, and God was with me?

5. Look back at a past darkness by the light of day. What dangers do you now see that God kept you from?

A PRAYER
Lord, You have not promised to keep me out of the valley, but You have promised to be with me in it. When I cannot see where to put my foot, hold me on the narrow way.
When the terrors overwhelm me and I have no words, hear my one cry: O Lord, deliver my soul.
When the enemy whispers blasphemies in my ear, let me know they are not mine, and let me run to You rather than examine myself.
Let me hear the voices of Your people ahead of me in the dark, and in Your time turn my shadow of death into the morning. Amen.

fields.title: Vanity Fair and Faithful
fields.body_html:
Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. 1 JOHN 2:15

Christian has overtaken Faithful, the voice ahead of him in the dark valley, and the two walk on together. Evangelist meets them once more and warns them plainly: they are about to come into a town where they will be hard beset, and one or both of them must seal their testimony with blood. Be faithful unto death, he says, and the King will give you a crown of life. Then they come out of the wilderness and see the town ahead. Its name is Vanity, and in it there is a fair kept all the year long, called Vanity Fair.

A fair that never closes

Bunyan tells us the history of the fair. Almost five thousand years ago, Beelzebub, Apollyon and Legion saw that the pilgrims’ path to the Celestial City lay through this town, and set up a fair there to sell all sorts of vanity. And what is sold? Houses, lands, trades, places, honours, preferments, titles, countries, kingdoms, lusts, pleasures and delights of all sorts; wives, husbands, children, masters, servants, lives, blood, bodies, souls, silver, gold and precious stones. There are rows for every nation. There are jugglings, cheats, games and plays, and — to be seen for nothing — thefts, murders and adulteries.

Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity. ECCLESIASTES 1:2

The list is deliberately jumbled. Crowns and lusts, souls and silver, children and servants, all laid out on the same stalls. That is the genius of the picture. In Vanity Fair everything has a price, including things that should never be bought and sold — people, bodies, souls. The fair does not only sell sin; it turns good things into merchandise. A family becomes a status symbol; a career becomes an idol; a soul becomes a commodity. Much of the modern economy of attention would have been perfectly familiar to Bunyan.

And there is no way round it. The way to the Celestial City lies right through this town, and anyone who would avoid it must needs go out of the world. Christ Himself went through it, on a fair-day too, and Beelzebub led Him from street to street and offered to make Him lord of the fair if He would do him reverence. But He had no mind to the merchandise, and left the town without laying out so much as one farthing.

Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; and saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me. MATTHEW 4:8–9

Why the pilgrims caused a riot

As soon as Christian and Faithful enter the fair, the whole town is in a hubbub, and Bunyan gives three reasons. First, their clothes are different; people call them fools, bedlams and outlandish men. Second, their speech is different; they naturally speak the language of Canaan, and the men of the fair cannot understand them. Third, and most offensive of all, they set very light by the wares. They will not even look at them. When called to buy, they put their fingers in their ears and cry, Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity, and look upward.

Then someone mockingly asks, “What will ye buy?” And they look gravely at him and say, “We buy the truth.”

Buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding. PROVERBS 23:23

Notice that the pilgrims do nothing violent or even particularly provocative. They do not overturn the stalls or preach in the market. They simply refuse to be customers. That is what the world cannot forgive. A Christian who shares the world’s desires in a slightly more respectable form causes no stir at all. A Christian who plainly does not want what the world is selling is a standing rebuke.

The trial

The pilgrims are beaten, smeared with dirt and put in a cage as a spectacle. They bear it patiently, blessing those who curse them, and some in the fair begin to take their part, which only makes things worse. At last they are brought to trial before the judge, Lord Hate-good, charged with being enemies to the trade and disturbers of the town.

Three witnesses testify against Faithful: Envy, Superstition and Pickthank — a flatterer. Envy says Faithful holds that Christianity and the customs of the town are diametrically opposite and cannot be reconciled. Faithful answers boldly. The jury is made up of Mr Blindman, Mr No-good, Mr Malice, Mr Love-lust, Mr Live-loose, Mr Heady, Mr High-mind, Mr Enmity, Mr Liar, Mr Cruelty, Mr Hate-light and Mr Implacable, and they bring him in guilty with one voice.

Readers in Bunyan’s day would have known what he was doing. He had himself stood before justices and been sentenced for refusing to conform. The indictment against the pilgrims — making commotions and divisions, winning a party to dangerous opinions, contempt of the law of their prince — has the ring of the charges against Dissenters in Restoration England. Vanity Fair is not only the world in general. It is the world at the moment it becomes a persecutor.

Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. 2 TIMOTHY 3:12

Faithful’s death

Faithful is scourged, buffeted, lanced with knives, stoned, pricked with swords, and burned to ashes at the stake. But behind the crowd stands a chariot and a couple of horses waiting for him, and as soon as his enemies have finished, he is taken up into it and carried through the clouds with the sound of a trumpet, the nearest way to the celestial gate.

Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. REVELATION 2:10

It is one of the most moving moments in the book, and it is also profoundly consoling. Evangelist had told them that the one who died at Vanity Fair would have the better of his fellow, because he would reach the city soonest and escape many miseries on the road. What looks like defeat to the fair is, to heaven, the quickest way home. Bunyan wrote those words in the knowledge that he himself might be hanged.

Hopeful rises from the ashes

Christian is remanded to prison and, by the overruling of Him who rules all things, escapes. But he does not go on alone. A man named Hopeful, made so by watching Christian and Faithful in their words and behaviour and their sufferings at the fair, joins himself to him in a brotherly covenant. Thus, says Bunyan, one died to bear testimony to the truth, and another rose out of his ashes to be a companion to Christian. Hopeful tells him that many more men in the fair will take their time and follow after.

Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit. JOHN 12:24
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Walk through a street, a shopping centre or across a screen this week and notice the wares of Vanity Fair. Which stalls call to you most?

2. Ask honestly: would anyone at the fair notice that you are a pilgrim? In what one way could your clothing, speech or spending be more plainly Christ’s?

3. Pray for Christians on trial or in prison for their faith today, and for those who judge them.

4. Is there a place in your life where you are expected to buy what the world is selling? Practise the answer: I buy the truth.

5. Think of someone whose faithfulness under pressure made you a pilgrim. Thank God for them.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You walked through Vanity Fair and bought nothing, though its lord offered You all the kingdoms of the world.
Turn away my eyes from beholding vanity. Give me a love for the truth that makes the world’s wares seem light.
Make me different enough to be noticed, patient enough to bear reproach, and faithful enough to die rather than deny You.
And let my faithfulness, like Faithful’s, raise up hope in others who are watching. Amen.

If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. 1 JOHN 2:15 Christian has overtaken Faithful, the voice ahead of him in the dark valley, and the two walk on together. Evangelist meets them once more and warns them plainly: they are about to come into a town where they will be hard beset, and one or both of them must seal their testimony with blood. Be faithful unto death, he says, and the King will give you a crown of life. Then they come out of the wilderness and see the town ahead. Its name is Vanity, and in it there is a fair kept all the year long, called Vanity Fair. A fair that never closes Bunyan tells us the history of the fair. Almost five thousand years ago, Beelzebub, Apollyon and Legion saw that the pilgrims’ path to the Celestial City lay through this town, and set up a fair there to sell all sorts of vanity. And what is sold? Houses, lands, trades, places, honours, preferments, titles, countries, kingdoms, lusts, pleasures and delights of all sorts; wives, husbands, children, masters, servants, lives, blood, bodies, souls, silver, gold and precious stones. There are rows for every nation. There are jugglings, cheats, games and plays, and — to be seen for nothing — thefts, murders and adulteries. Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity. ECCLESIASTES 1:2 The list is deliberately jumbled. Crowns and lusts, souls and silver, children and servants, all laid out on the same stalls. That is the genius of the picture. In Vanity Fair everything has a price, including things that should never be bought and sold — people, bodies, souls. The fair does not only sell sin; it turns good things into merchandise. A family becomes a status symbol; a career becomes an idol; a soul becomes a commodity. Much of the modern economy of attention would have been perfectly familiar to Bunyan. And there is no way round it. The way to the Celestial City lies right through this town, and anyone who would avoid it must needs go out of the world. Christ Himself went through it, on a fair-day too, and Beelzebub led Him from street to street and offered to make Him lord of the fair if He would do him reverence. But He had no mind to the merchandise, and left the town without laying out so much as one farthing. Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; and saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me. Second, their speech is different; they naturally speak the language of Canaan, and the men of the fair cannot understand them. Third, and most offensive of all, they set very light by the wares. Walk through a street, a shopping centre or across a screen this week and notice the wares of Vanity Fair. Which stalls call to you most? 2. Ask honestly: would anyone at the fair notice that you are a pilgrim? In what one way could your clothing, speech or spending be more plainly Christ’s? 3. Pray for Christians on trial or in prison for their faith today, and for those who judge them. 4. Is there a place in your life where you are expected to buy what the world is selling? Practise the answer: I buy the truth. 5. Think of someone whose faithfulness under pressure made you a pilgrim. Thank God for them. Give me a love for the truth that makes the world’s wares seem light. Make me different enough to be noticed, patient enough to bear reproach, and faithful enough to die rather than deny You. fields.title: Religion in Silver Slippers
fields.body_html:
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away. 2 TIMOTHY 3:5

The Pilgrim’s Progress is crowded with false pilgrims. Some are comic, some pitiable, some sinister. Bunyan spent more ink on them than on almost anything else, and it is not hard to see why. The danger he feared most for his readers was not open unbelief. It was a religion that looked like the real thing and was not. Two of these counterfeits stand out: Talkative, whom Christian and Faithful meet before Vanity Fair, and By-ends, whom Christian and Hopeful meet just after it.

Talkative: saying and doing

Talkative is a tall man, better looking at a distance than near at hand, and he can talk about anything — heaven and earth, law and gospel, the new birth, the insufficiency of works, the need of Christ’s righteousness. Faithful is charmed. Christian, who knows him from the City of Destruction, is not. Talkative, he says, is a saint abroad and a devil at home. His religion is all in his tongue. His family, his servants and those who do business with him know him for a churl and a cheat.

So Faithful puts a searching question to him: how does the saving grace of God show itself in the heart? Talkative answers glibly that it causes a great outcry against sin. Faithful replies that a man may cry out against sin and still harbour it, and that grace shows itself rather by inclining the soul to abhor its sin, and by a life that answers to what is known. When Faithful presses him about his own life, Talkative takes offence and leaves.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

Christian sums it up in a sentence: “The soul of religion is the practical part.” Hearing, he goes on, is but the sowing of the seed; talking is not enough to prove that fruit is in the heart; and at the last day men will not be asked whether they believed, but whether they were doers or talkers only.

By-ends of Fair-speech

Just out of Vanity Fair, Christian and Hopeful overtake a man from the town of Fair-speech. He is reluctant to give his name, but it turns out to be By-ends — a by-end being a secondary, selfish purpose. He is well connected. His kindred include my Lord Turn-about, my Lord Time-server, my Lord Fair-speech, Mr Smooth-man, Mr Facing-both-ways and Mr Anything, and the parson of the parish, Mr Two-tongues, is his uncle. His great-grandfather was a waterman, looking one way and rowing another, and By-ends has made most of his estate the same way.

By-ends is perfectly willing to be a pilgrim. He differs from the stricter sort, he says, in only two small points. First, he never strives against wind and tide. Second, he is always most zealous when religion goes in his silver slippers; he loves much to walk with religion in the street, if the sun shines and the people applaud.

Christian answers him plainly: “If you will go with us, you must go against wind and tide.” He must own religion in his rags as well as in his silver slippers, and stand by him when bound in irons as well as when he walks the streets with applause.

And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. LUKE 9:23

By-ends will not. He falls behind and is joined by three old schoolfellows, Mr Hold-the-world, Mr Money-love and Mr Save-all, all taught by one Mr Gripe-man, a schoolmaster in the market town of Love-gain in the county of Coveting. They agree that the pilgrims ahead are rigid and headstrong, and that the wise man is for religion only so far as the times and his safety will bear it.

Religion as a stalking-horse

Then the schoolfellows discuss a case of conscience. Suppose a minister has a small living and sees the chance of a bigger one, if he becomes more studious, preaches more zealously and alters some of his principles to suit the people. May he do it? Or suppose a tradesman can get a rich wife and more customers by becoming religious. Mr Money-love argues that he may, for it makes him a better man and brings good to others too. They all applaud, and put the question to Christian and Hopeful, expecting to silence them.

Christian answers that a babe in religion could answer ten thousand such questions. If it is unlawful to follow Christ for loaves, as it is, how much more abominable is it to make of Him and religion a stalking-horse to get and enjoy the world. He lists those in Scripture who took that view: Hamor and Shechem, who were circumcised to get Jacob’s cattle; the Pharisees, who made long prayers for a pretence to devour widows’ houses; Judas, who was religious for the bag; Simon Magus, who wanted the Holy Ghost to make money by it. The schoolfellows stand staring at one another, and have nothing to answer.

Jesus answered them and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Ye seek me, not because ye saw the miracles, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled. JOHN 6:26

It is a sharp word for every generation. There are always those who use religion as a ladder: for reputation, for business, for politics, for influence. The prosperity preaching of our own day, which promises wealth and health to the faithful, is only a louder version of Mr Money-love’s argument. And the temptation is not only for others. Every Christian must ask how much of his religion would survive if it brought him nothing but rags and irons.

The hill called Lucre

Soon after, the pilgrims cross a pleasant plain called Ease, and beyond it a little hill called Lucre, with a silver mine in it. A gentlemanly man named Demas stands by the road calling them to turn aside and dig. Some who went near the brim before them fell in and were slain; others were maimed and never their own men again. Christian refuses; Hopeful is tempted and says, let us go and see, but Christian will not stir a step, and talks him out of it. By-ends and his friends come up behind, go over to Demas at the first call, and are never seen in the way again.

For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world. 2 TIMOTHY 4:10

Just beyond the hill stands an old monument: a pillar in the shape of a woman — Lot’s wife, turned to salt for looking back towards Sodom. Hopeful is sobered. She only looked back, he says, and he had a desire to go and see. Christian draws the lesson: remember Lot’s wife.

Weighing ourselves

Bunyan does not want his readers to spend their time spotting By-ends in other people. The point of every counterfeit in the book is self-examination. Talkative asks whether our religion is in our tongue or our life. By-ends asks whether we follow Christ only when the sun shines. Mr Money-love asks whether our faith has quietly become a means to other ends. Demas asks what silver mine we are tempted to turn aside to see.

Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. 2 CORINTHIANS 13:5
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where is your religion more talk than practice? Choose one thing you often speak about and resolve to do it this week.

2. Ask the people who live with you whether you are the same at home as you are at church. Listen humbly.

3. Would you still follow Christ if it cost you your reputation, income or friendships? Name the thing you would find hardest to lose.

4. Examine one area — work, politics, social standing — where you may be using religion as a stalking-horse.

5. What is your hill called Lucre? Decide in advance not to turn aside to look.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You were despised and rejected, and You walked in rags, not silver slippers. Forgive me for wanting You only when the sun shines.
Deliver me from a religion of the tongue. Make my life speak louder than my talk, especially at home.
Keep me from using You to get the world, and from turning aside to any silver mine.
Give me grace to go with You against wind and tide, and to own You in Your rags as well as in Your glory. Amen.

fields.title: Doubting Castle and the Key Called Promise
fields.body_html:
For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us. 2 CORINTHIANS 1:20

Some of Bunyan’s best-loved scenes are his darkest. After the pleasant river with its fruit trees and meadows, the way grows rough, and the pilgrims’ feet are sore. On the left of the road is a meadow, and a stile over into it, and a path running along beside the way, soft and easy. It is called By-path Meadow. Christian thinks it runs alongside the way and persuades Hopeful to cross with him. It is the beginning of the worst captivity in the book.

Out of the way through a stile

The mistake is small, and it is Christian’s. He is the older pilgrim, and Hopeful follows him, though with a gentle caution. They meet a man called Vain-Confidence going the same way, who assures them it leads to the Celestial Gate. Then night falls; Vain-Confidence, walking ahead in the dark, falls into a deep pit and is dashed to pieces; the rain comes down, the waters rise, and the two pilgrims, trying to get back, are nearly drowned nine or ten times. At last they shelter and fall asleep — in the grounds of Doubting Castle, whose owner is Giant Despair.

There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death. PROVERBS 16:25

Bunyan is precise about how despair comes. It does not usually come from great crimes. It comes from a small turning aside to an easier path, a little self-confidence, a night in the wrong place. And there is a moment of real tenderness in the dark: Christian, ashamed, asks Hopeful to forgive him for leading him out of the way, and Hopeful does, and adds that he believes this shall be for their good. Even in the worst hours, the pilgrims do not turn on each other.

The giant and his wife

In the morning Giant Despair finds them asleep in his grounds and drives them into a very dark, nasty and stinking dungeon, where they lie from Wednesday morning till Saturday night without bread, drink or light. His wife, whose name is Diffidence, counsels him to beat them without mercy, and he does, with a grievous crab-tree cudgel. The next night she advises him to urge them to make away with themselves.

This is the most painful part of the whole book, and it must be read with care. Giant Despair tells the prisoners that since they are never likely to come out, their only way is to make an end of themselves, with knife, halter or poison. And Christian, the hero of the story, the man who fought Apollyon, begins to agree. My soul chooseth strangling rather than life, he says, quoting Job; the grave is easier than this dungeon.

So that my soul chooseth strangling, and death rather than my life. JOB 7:15

Hopeful’s counsel

It is Hopeful — the younger, weaker pilgrim — who holds on. He reminds Christian that the Lord of the country they are going to has said, Thou shalt do no murder, and that this forbids a man to kill himself as much as another. He reminds him that others have escaped from his hands, and that God who made the world may yet cause the giant to die or forget to lock the door. Let us be patient, he says, and endure a while; the time may come when we are given a happy release.

The next night, when Christian again wavers, Hopeful reminds him how valiant he has been before: Apollyon could not crush him, nor the terrors of the Valley of the Shadow. He, Hopeful, is a far weaker man by nature, and yet is in the dungeon with him. Remember how you played the man at Vanity Fair, he says, and were neither afraid of the chain, nor cage, nor bloody death; let us at least avoid the shame that becomes not a Christian to be found in.

Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God. PSALM 42:11

If you are in that dungeon now, and the thought of ending your life has come to you, please do what Christian did: tell someone who is with you. Speak to a friend, a pastor, a doctor, or a crisis helpline today. The giant is lying to you. There is a way out.

The key in his bosom

On Saturday about midnight the pilgrims begin to pray, and continue in prayer till almost break of day. And a little before dawn Christian breaks out, as one half amazed: “What a fool, quoth he, am I, thus to lie in a stinking dungeon, when I may as well walk at liberty! I have a key in my bosom, called Promise, that will, I am persuaded, open any lock in Doubting Castle.”

Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature. 2 PETER 1:4

Hopeful says, good news, brother; pluck it out and try. The key turns the lock of the dungeon door, and the door flies open with ease. It opens the door into the castle yard. It opens the iron gate — though that lock goes desperately hard. The gate creaks, the giant wakes to pursue them, but his fits take him and his limbs fail, and the pilgrims run back to the King’s highway.

There are three things to notice. First, Christian had the key all along. It was in his bosom the whole time he lay in the dungeon. The promises of God do not go away when we despair; we simply forget we have them. Second, the key was found after a night of prayer. Third, the last lock was the hardest. Deliverance from despair is not always easy, even with the promise in hand. But the key did open it.

And this is the promise that he hath promised us, even eternal life. 1 JOHN 2:25

A pillar for those who come after

Back over the stile, the pilgrims set up a pillar with a warning engraved on it: that over this stile is the way to Doubting Castle, kept by Giant Despair. Many who came after read it and escaped. The first thing Christian and Hopeful do with their freedom is to protect others. Those who have been in the dungeon are the best people to warn the rest — and, in the Second Part, Great-heart and his company come back this way and pull Doubting Castle down.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. What is your By-path Meadow — the small easier path that runs alongside the way and leads off it?

2. Write down three promises of God and keep them in your bosom — in your pocket, phone or memory — for the day you need a key.

3. If you are in a dungeon of despair, tell one person this week. If you have had any thought of ending your life, speak to someone today.

4. Is there a Christian near you in Doubting Castle? Be their Hopeful: remind them of God’s command, His power and His past faithfulness, and stay with them.

5. If God has brought you out, set up a pillar: warn someone else of the stile that led you in.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have stepped over the stile into easier paths, and found myself in the dungeon of despair. Forgive me, and do not leave me there.
When the giant tells me there is no way out, give me a friend like Hopeful, and make me a friend like him to others.
Remind me of the key in my bosom. Let Your promises open every lock, even the one that goes desperately hard.
Bring me back to the King’s highway, and let me warn those who come after me. Amen.

It comes from a small turning aside to an easier path, a little self-confidence, a night in the wrong place. And there is a moment of real tenderness in the dark: Christian, ashamed, asks Hopeful to forgive him for leading him out of the way, and Hopeful does, and adds that he believes this shall be for their good. First, Christian had the key all along. It was in his bosom the whole time he lay in the dungeon. The promises of God do not go away when we despair; we simply forget we have them. Second, the key was found after a night of prayer. Third, the last lock was the hardest. Deliverance from despair is not always easy, even with the promise in hand. But the key did open it. Many who came after read it and escaped. The first thing Christian and Hopeful do with their freedom is to protect others. Those who have been in the dungeon are the best people to warn the rest — and, in the Second Part, Great-heart and his company come back this way and pull Doubting Castle down. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. What is your By-path Meadow — the small easier path that runs alongside the way and leads off it? 2. Write down three promises of God and keep them in your bosom — in your pocket, phone or memory — for the day you need a key. 3. If you are in a dungeon of despair, tell one person this week. If you have had any thought of ending your life, speak to someone today. 4. Is there a Christian near you in Doubting Castle? Be their Hopeful: remind them of God’s command, His power and His past faithfulness, and stay with them. 5. If God has brought you out, set up a pillar: warn someone else of the stile that led you in. A PRAYER Lord, I have stepped over the stile into easier paths, and found myself in the dungeon of despair. Forgive me, and do not leave me there. When the giant tells me there is no way out, give me a friend like Hopeful, and make me a friend like him to others. Remind me of the key in my bosom. Let Your promises open every lock, even the one that goes desperately hard. Bring me back to the King’s highway, and let me warn those who come after me. Amen.

fields.title: The Delectable Mountains
fields.body_html:
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind. 1 PETER 5:2

Out of Doubting Castle, bruised and shaken, Christian and Hopeful come to the Delectable Mountains. They had seen them long before, far off, from the roof of the Palace Beautiful. Now they walk among their gardens, orchards, vineyards and fountains, drink and wash and eat freely. And on the tops of the mountains, by the highway side, shepherds are feeding their flocks.

Emmanuel’s land

The pilgrims, leaning on their staffs as weary travellers do, ask whose mountains these are and whose sheep. The shepherds answer: These mountains are Emmanuel’s land, and they are within sight of His city; and the sheep also are His, and He laid down His life for them.

I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. JOHN 10:11

Then the pilgrims ask their questions, and the answers are some of the most compressed wisdom in the book. Is this the way to the Celestial City? You are just in your way. How far is it? Too far for any but those who shall get thither indeed. Is the way safe or dangerous? Safe for those for whom it is to be safe, but transgressors shall fall therein.

These answers are not evasive. They are exactly true. The way is long, and only those who persevere reach the end. It is perfectly safe for those who walk in it, and deadly for those who leave it. Bunyan, a Calvinist, believed firmly that God keeps His own to the end. But he never let that belief make pilgrims careless. The shepherds say both things in the same breath.

Shepherds with names

The shepherds’ names are Knowledge, Experience, Watchful and Sincere. It is Bunyan’s second portrait of the faithful minister, after the picture in the Interpreter’s house, and this time there are four of them — a reminder that the care of souls is shared work. Between them they have the marks of a good pastor: knowledge of the truth, experience of its power, watchfulness over the flock, and sincerity of heart.

Before welcoming the pilgrims they ask them how they came into the way and by what means they have persevered, for, they say, few who begin ever show their faces on these mountains. Then they look very lovingly on them and say, Welcome to the Delectable Mountains. They take them to their tents, feed them, and ask them to stay a while.

And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding. JEREMIAH 3:15

Things shown from the hilltops

The next morning the shepherds take the pilgrims walking and show them some wonders — and most of them are warnings.

From the top of a hill called Error they look down and see men dashed to pieces at the bottom. These are those who erred concerning the resurrection, following the false teachers Hymenaeus and Philetus, and they lie unburied as an example to others to take heed how they clamber too high or come too near the brink of that mountain. Bunyan is warning against doctrinal error, and especially the kind that comes from clever speculation beyond Scripture.

Who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some. 2 TIMOTHY 2:18

From the top of a mountain called Caution they see blind men stumbling among tombs. These, the shepherds explain, came on pilgrimage as far as the stile into By-path Meadow, were taken by Giant Despair, and had their eyes put out and were left to wander. Christian and Hopeful look at one another with tears running down their cheeks, and say nothing. They know how close they came.

Then the shepherds open a door in the side of a hill, and inside is darkness, smoke, a rumbling as of fire and the smell of brimstone. This, they say, is a by-way to hell, a way that hypocrites go in at: those who sell their birthright with Esau, sell their Master with Judas, blaspheme the gospel with Alexander, and lie and dissemble with Ananias and Sapphira. Hopeful asks whether these all had a show of pilgrimage, as they have. Yes, say the shepherds, and held it a long time, too. And the pilgrims say to one another, We had need to cry to the Strong for strength. Aye, say the shepherds, and you will have need to use it when you have it, too.

Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. 1 CORINTHIANS 10:12

A word of care belongs here. It is striking that Bunyan, who for years was tormented by the fear that he was Esau and had sold his birthright, puts Esau at the door of this by-way. He does not say that everyone who fears he is Esau is Esau. On the contrary, Grace Abounding shows at length that such fear was itself a mark that he was not. The shepherds’ warning is for the careless hypocrite, not the trembling believer. If you fear that door, your fear is a sign that you are crying to the Strong for strength, and that is exactly what the shepherds commended.

The perspective glass

Last of all, the shepherds take them to a high hill called Clear and let them look through a perspective glass towards the gates of the Celestial City. But the memory of the by-way to hell makes their hands shake, and they cannot hold the glass steady. Yet they think they see something like the gate and some of the glory of the place.

For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known. 1 CORINTHIANS 13:12

A note of the way

As the pilgrims leave, one shepherd gives them a note of the way. Another bids them beware of the Flatterer. A third bids them take heed not to sleep on the Enchanted Ground. The fourth bids them Godspeed.

Almost at once they forget two of the four. They meet a man in a white robe who offers to lead them to the city, follow him, and find themselves caught in a net — he was the Flatterer. A Shining One frees them, asks why they did not read their note, and chastises them with a whip of small cords, to teach them the good way. And later, on the Enchanted Ground, where the air makes pilgrims drowsy, Hopeful wants to sleep, and Christian reminds him of the shepherds’ warning. They keep each other awake by talking of how God first dealt with their souls.

As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent. REVELATION 3:19
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Thank God for the pastors and older believers who have been Knowledge, Experience, Watchful and Sincere to you. Pray for one of them by name.

2. If you are weary after a hard season, let others care for you. Accept the welcome of the Delectable Mountains before you hurry on.

3. Which warning do you most need: Error, Caution, or the by-way to hell? Take it seriously without letting it become despair.

4. Spend time this week looking through the perspective glass: read Revelation 21–22 slowly and ask to see something of the glory.

5. Is there counsel a pastor or friend gave you that you have neglected? Go back to your note of the way.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, Chief Shepherd, these mountains are Your land, and the sheep are Yours, for You laid down Your life for them.
Thank You for the shepherds You have given me. Make me teachable, and give them knowledge, experience, watchfulness and sincerity.
When I see the warnings, let me cry to the Strong for strength; when I see the glory, however dimly, let me long for it.
Keep me from the Flatterer and from drowsiness, and correct me in love when I forget Your word. Amen.

fields.title: Ignorance and the Good Heart
fields.body_html:
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? JEREMIAH 17:9

Of all the false pilgrims in the First Part, Ignorance is the one Bunyan follows furthest — all the way to the gate of the Celestial City. He is not a villain, a hypocrite or a scoffer. He is pleasant, confident, religious and sincere. And the last sentence of the dream is about him.

A brisk lad from Conceit

Just below the Delectable Mountains, a little crooked lane comes into the way from the country of Conceit, and down it comes a very brisk lad whose name is Ignorance. He is going to the Celestial City. Christian asks how he expects to get in at the gate. “As other good people do,” he says. And what will he show at the gate? He knows his Lord’s will, he says, and has been a good liver; he pays every man his own, prays, fasts, pays tithes, gives alms, and has left his country for where he is going.

Christian points out that he did not come in at the wicket gate but by the crooked lane, and may be counted a thief and a robber at the end. Ignorance is unbothered. Christian and Hopeful are strangers to him; let them follow the religion of their country, and he will follow the religion of his. As for the gate, all the world knows it is a great way off; they have a fine, pleasant green lane that comes down the next way into the way.

Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 7:21

My heart tells me so

On the Enchanted Ground Christian and Hopeful fall back and talk with Ignorance at length, and this conversation is the theological heart of the First Part.

Christian asks how things stand between God and his soul. Well, says Ignorance; he is always full of good motions that come into his mind to comfort him as he walks. He thinks of God and heaven, and desires them, and leaves all for them. How does he know he has left all? “My heart tells me so.” Christian quotes Proverbs: he that trusteth in his own heart is a fool. That is spoken of an evil heart, says Ignorance, but mine is a good one. How does he know? Because his heart and life agree together.

He that trusteth in his own heart is a fool: but whoso walketh wisely, he shall be delivered. PROVERBS 28:26

Christian then explains what a good heart and good thoughts really are. Good thoughts about ourselves are those that agree with the word of God — and the word says that there is none righteous, that the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth. When we think of ourselves so, and feel it, our thoughts are good ones, because they agree with God’s judgement. Ignorance replies, “I will never believe that my heart is thus bad.”

A faith of his own making

Then Christian asks about his faith in Christ. Ignorance says he believes that Christ died for sinners, and that he shall be justified before God from the curse through Christ’s gracious acceptance of his obedience to His laws. Or, he adds, Christ makes his religious duties acceptable to the Father by virtue of His merits.

Christian’s answer is careful and precise. This is a fantastical faith, he says, for it is nowhere described in the word. It is a false faith, because it takes justification from the personal righteousness of Christ and applies it to Ignorance’s own. It makes Christ a justifier of his actions rather than of his person. True faith, by contrast, flies for refuge to Christ’s own righteousness — His personal obedience to the law, in doing and suffering for us — and, shrouded under the skirt of it, the soul is presented spotless before God and acquitted.

And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith. PHILIPPIANS 3:9

This is the doctrine of justification by the imputed righteousness of Christ, and it lay at the centre of Bunyan’s whole life. It is exactly what he discovered in the field outside Bedford, when the sentence fell on his soul that his righteousness was in heaven. Ignorance’s faith sounds very like the gospel. It mentions Christ, His death and His merits. But it quietly puts the believer’s own obedience back at the centre, with Christ as a kind of helper who tops it up. Bunyan saw that the difference was the difference between heaven and hell.

Ignorance objects at once: would you have us trust to what Christ in His own person has done without us? That would loosen the reins of our lusts and let us live as we please. Christian replies that Ignorance is ignorant of the true effects of saving faith, which bows and wins the heart to God in Christ, to love His name, His word, His ways and His people. Grace does not make us careless. It makes us grateful.

Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein? ROMANS 6:1–2

A way to hell from heaven’s gate

We do not see Ignorance again until the very end. After Christian and Hopeful have crossed the river with great difficulty and entered the city in glory, the dreamer looks back and sees Ignorance come to the riverside. He gets over easily, without half the difficulty the others had, because a ferryman named Vain-Hope takes him across in his boat. He climbs the hill alone; no one meets him with the least encouragement. He knocks, expecting to be let in quickly. Asked for his certificate, he fumbles in his bosom and finds none. The King will not come down to see him, but commands that he be bound hand and foot and taken away to the door in the side of the hill.

And then the dream ends with a sentence that has haunted readers for three hundred years: “Then I saw that there was a way to hell, even from the gate of heaven, as well as from the City of Destruction.”

Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? … And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you. MATTHEW 7:22–23

Reading this with care

This is a severe ending, and it is meant to be. But notice who it is aimed at. It is aimed at the self-confident, not the self-doubting. Ignorance crosses the river easily and knocks expecting welcome; Christian nearly drowns in the river, full of fears. The one who is lost is the one who never doubted himself. If you are anxious about whether you have true faith, you are, in that respect at least, very unlike Ignorance. The remedy for your fear is the same as the remedy for his confidence: look away from your own heart to Christ’s righteousness.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where does your own hope of heaven rest? Write it in one sentence. Does it mention your heart, your life, or Christ’s righteousness?

2. Read Philippians 3:4–9 and list what Paul counted loss. Is anything on your own list?

3. Think of someone you love who, like Ignorance, assumes good people go to heaven. Pray for them, and look for a gentle way to speak of Christ’s righteousness.

4. If you fear you might be Ignorance, notice the difference between his confidence and your concern, and bring your concern to Christ.

5. Ask God to show you the true state of your heart, and then to show you Christ.

A PRAYER
Lord, my heart is deceitful, and I have often trusted it. Forgive me for thinking myself good and my religion sufficient.
Deliver me from a faith of my own making. Let me be found in Christ, not having my own righteousness, but His.
Let His righteousness win my heart, so that I love Your name, Your word, Your ways and Your people.
And have mercy on those who walk the pleasant green lane of Conceit. Open their eyes before they come to the river. Amen.

fields.title: The River and the Celestial City
fields.body_html:
When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee. ISAIAH 43:2

Every road in The Pilgrim’s Progress leads, in the end, to the river. After the Enchanted Ground the pilgrims come into the country of Beulah, where the air is sweet, the birds sing, the sun shines night and day, and they are out of sight of Doubting Castle. They can see the city now, built of pearls and precious stones, so glorious that Christian falls sick with longing. Two men in raiment that shines like gold meet them and tell them they have but two difficulties more, and then they are in the city. Between them and the gate is a river. There is no bridge, and the river is very deep.

There is no bridge

The pilgrims are stunned. They ask whether there is no other way to the gate. Only two, they are told, Enoch and Elijah, have been permitted to tread another path since the foundation of the world. Christian begins to despond. They ask whether the waters are all of one depth. No, say the men; you shall find it deeper or shallower as you believe in the King of the place.

For I know that thou wilt bring me to death, and to the house appointed for all living. JOB 30:23

The river is death, and Bunyan is honest about it. There is no way round. Every pilgrim, however far he has come, however many battles he has won, must go through the water. And the depth of the river is not the same for all. It depends on faith — or rather, on how far the pilgrim is able, in that hour, to lean on the King.

I sink in deep waters

They go into the water, and Christian begins to sink. He cries out to his good friend Hopeful, I sink in deep waters; the billows go over my head; all his waves go over me. Hopeful answers with one of the most comforting sentences in the book: “Be of good cheer, my brother: I feel the bottom, and it is good.”

But Christian cannot feel it. A great darkness and horror falls on him, so that he cannot see before him. He loses his senses in great measure, and cannot remember any of the sweet refreshments he met on the way. He is troubled by the thought of the sins he committed, both before and since he became a pilgrim, and by apparitions of hobgoblins and evil spirits. Hopeful has much ado to keep his brother’s head above water.

Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul. PSALM 69:1

This is astonishing, and it is deliberate. Christian — the man who lost his burden at the cross, fought Apollyon, walked through the Valley of the Shadow, stood firm at Vanity Fair — dies in terror. Bunyan does not give his hero a serene deathbed. He gives him the deathbed that many real saints have had: dark, confused, full of fear and old guilt. And Bunyan is saying to every believer who dreads dying badly: it is no sign that God has forsaken you.

These troubles are no sign

Hopeful tries to comfort him. Brother, I see the gate, and men standing by to receive us. Christian answers, It is you they wait for; you have been hopeful ever since I knew you. If I were right, surely He would now arise to help me; but for my sins He has brought me into the snare and left me.

Then Hopeful gives him the answer that has comforted dying Christians for centuries. You have forgotten the text, he says, that speaks of the wicked, that there are no bands in their death, but their strength is firm. And then, in Bunyan’s own words: “These troubles and distresses that you go through in these waters, are no sign that God hath forsaken you; but are sent to try you” — to see whether you will call to mind the goodness you have already received from Him, and live upon Him in your distress.

For there are no bands in their death: but their strength is firm. They are not in trouble as other men; neither are they plagued like other men. PSALM 73:4–5

I see Him again

Christian is in a muse a while. Then Hopeful adds, Be of good cheer, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole. And Christian breaks out with a loud voice: Oh, I see Him again; and He tells me, When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee. Then they both take courage, the enemy is as still as a stone, Christian finds ground to stand on, and the rest of the river is shallow. Thus they get over.

O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:55–57

The welcome

On the other bank the Shining Ones wait for them. The pilgrims have left their mortal garments in the river; they went in with them and came out without. They go up the mighty hill with ease, led by the arms, sweetly talking as they go. A company of the heavenly host comes out to meet them; the King’s trumpeters salute them with ten thousand welcomes. They give in their certificates — the rolls received at the cross — and the King commands the gate to be opened. As they enter, they are transfigured, clothed in raiment that shines like gold, given harps and crowns, and all the bells of the city ring for joy.

And I heard a great voice out of heaven saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God. REVELATION 21:3

The dreamer looks in after them and sees the city shining like the sun, and those within singing Holy, holy, holy is the Lord. Then the gates are shut. And, he says, “when I had seen, I wished myself among them.”

The deaths in the Second Part

Bunyan returned to the river at the end of the Second Part, and there the tone is different. The pilgrims in Christiana’s company receive their summons one by one, and most go over in peace. Mr Standfast, halfway in, stands and talks with his friends. “This river has been a terror to many,” he says; the thoughts of it had often frightened him; but now his foot is fixed where the priests who bore the ark stood when Israel crossed Jordan. Mr Valiant-for-truth leaves his sword to him that shall succeed him, and goes down into the water saying, Death, where is thy sting? and as he goes deeper, Grave, where is thy victory? “So he passed over, and all the trumpets sounded for him on the other side.”

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Have you thought honestly about your own death? Read Psalm 23 and 1 Corinthians 15:50–58, and let them shape your thoughts.

2. If you fear dying badly — in confusion, pain or doubt — take Hopeful’s words as God’s word to you: such troubles are no sign that He has forsaken you.

3. Choose one promise of Scripture to be the one you want spoken to you at the end, and tell someone who may be with you.

4. Be a Hopeful for a dying friend. Visit someone who is ill or old this month, and bring them a promise.

5. Spend a few minutes imagining the welcome — the bells, the trumpets, the King’s face — and let it strengthen you for today’s stretch of road.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You went through the river before me, and You have promised to be with me in the waters.
When I come to die, keep my head above the waves. If darkness falls and I forget Your mercies, send me a friend to speak Your word, and let me see You again.
Keep me from the false comfort of Vain-Hope, and give me the true comfort of Your promise.
And bring me safe over, to the city where the bells ring, and where I shall see You face to face. Amen.

fields.title: Sell Him, Sell Him
fields.body_html:
Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not. LUKE 22:31–32

We now leave the dream for the dreamer. At the centre of Grace Abounding is a temptation so strange and so terrible that many readers find it hard to believe. It is also one of the most pastorally important passages in Christian autobiography, because it describes with complete honesty a torment that many sincere believers still endure in silence.

This chapter needs a word of care at the outset. If you are prone to anxious, obsessive fears about your salvation, read it slowly, perhaps with a friend, and keep going to the end. Bunyan did come out. And the way he came out is the point.

A year of one sentence

It began, Bunyan says, after God had settled him sweetly in the faith and given him strong consolation. Then the tempter came again with a more grievous temptation than before: to sell and part with Christ, to exchange Him for the things of this life, for anything. It lay on him for about a year, so continually that he was not rid of it one day in a month. He could not eat his food, stoop for a pin, chop a stick or look at anything without the thought coming: Sell Christ for this, or sell Christ for that; sell Him, sell Him.

He fought it with all his strength. Sometimes his very body moved with the effort, pushing and thrusting with his hands and elbows, while he answered as fast as the destroyer spoke: “I will not, I will not, I will not, I will not; no, not for thousands, thousands, thousands of worlds.”

Then one morning, lying in bed, assaulted again, he answered no twenty times together until he was almost out of breath. And at last he felt the thought pass through his heart, Let Him go, if He will! — and thought he felt his heart freely consent. “Now was the battle won,” he writes, “and down I fell, as a bird that is shot from the top of a tree, into great guilt, and fearful despair.”

Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. For ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears. HEBREWS 12:16–17

Two years under Esau

What followed was two years in which, he says, nothing would abide with him but damnation and the expectation of damnation. The verse about Esau lay on him all day, all week, all year. He was certain he had committed the unpardonable sin. He compared himself with Judas and was ashamed to be like such an ugly man. He could scarcely look at a good man without trembling. He was weary of his life and yet afraid to die.

If we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin. 1 JOHN 1:7

What was really happening

Read with modern eyes, much of what Bunyan describes looks like what doctors today would call obsessive-compulsive disorder in its religious form — often called scrupulosity. Intrusive, unwanted thoughts, horrifying to the person who has them; a desperate struggle to neutralise them; the conviction that a single thought has consented and all is lost; endless checking of one’s own heart for evidence. Bunyan even records the tempter urging him, as he sat at his meals, to leave his food and go and pray at once, or he would displease God — and then, when he refused, feeling as guilty as if he had broken God’s law. He calls that devil counterfeit holy.

We should be careful not to explain Bunyan away. He was a man in real spiritual conflict, and he interpreted it in the categories of his time. But it is a mercy to know that such torment is well understood, that it is not a sign of reprobation, and that it can be helped. If this describes you, please speak to a pastor who understands it, and do not be afraid to see a doctor as well. Your fear that you have committed the unforgivable sin is not evidence that you have. It is almost always evidence that you have not.

The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. MATTHEW 26:41

How the Scriptures changed their faces

How did Bunyan come out? Not quickly, and not by a single experience, but by the slow work of God’s word.

First, God sent him promises, and they fought with the threats. Once, in a meeting of God’s people, full of terror, he heard with great power, My grace is sufficient for thee, three times over, and it was as though he saw the Lord Jesus look down from heaven through the tiles upon him. For weeks the promise of grace and the verse about Esau hung in his mind like a pair of scales. One day, he says, he longed that both scriptures might come upon him at once, to see which would get the better. They did, two or three days later, and at last the Esau verse grew weak and withdrew, and the word of grace prevailed. Then Mercy rejoiceth against judgment came home to him.

For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment. JAMES 2:13

Second, and crucially, he found the courage to look closely at the verses that terrified him. For a long time he could hardly bear to cast his eye on them, and had much ado an hundred times not to wish them out of the Bible. But when he finally read them with care, he says, he found their visage changed; they looked not so grimly on him as before. The falling away of Hebrews 6 was an open and absolute denial of the gospel. The wilful sin of Hebrews 10 was one that throws off Christ altogether with despite to the Spirit. And Esau’s sin was not a hasty thought against the continual labour of his mind, but a deliberate, public act, persisted in without regret. Bunyan’s passing thought, fought against with all his strength, was nothing of the kind.

Wherefore I say unto you, All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men. MATTHEW 12:31

Third, he received a searching question. Walking in a good man’s shop, ready to sink with fear, he seemed to hear a voice asking, Didst ever refuse to be justified by the blood of Christ? His whole past was opened to him, and he saw that he never had. That was the question that mattered. Not how strongly had he felt, nor whether a thought had passed through him, but whether he had ever refused Christ.

Great sins to draw out great grace

When it was over, Bunyan did not regret the storm. “I never saw those heights and depths in grace, and love, and mercy,” he writes, “as I saw after this temptation.” Great sins, he says, draw out great grace; and where guilt is most terrible, there the mercy of God in Christ appears most high and mighty.

Many are the afflictions of the righteous: but the LORD delivereth him out of them all. PSALM 34:19
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. If you have ever feared that you committed the unpardonable sin, ask Bunyan’s question: have I ever refused to be justified by the blood of Christ? If the answer is no, rest there.

2. If intrusive, unwanted thoughts torment you, tell a pastor who understands scrupulosity, and consider seeing a doctor. Seeking help is not a failure of faith.

3. Identify any verse you have avoided because it frightens you. Read it this week in its context, with a good commentary or a wise friend.

4. Memorise 2 Corinthians 12:9 and 1 John 1:7 as promises to set on the other side of the scales.

5. If God has brought you through a dark season, write down what He did, as Bunyan did, so that it may one day help someone else.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You prayed for Peter when Satan desired to sift him, and You pray for me. When my mind is assaulted with thoughts I hate, hold me fast.
Where the enemy tells me I have sold You, remind me that I have never refused Your blood, and that You will in no wise cast me out.
Let Your grace be sufficient for me, and let Your mercy rejoice against judgement.
Deliver those who are tormented as Bunyan was. Give them wise friends and patient help, and bring them out, as You brought him, into the light. Amen.

fields.title: Thy Righteousness Is in Heaven
fields.body_html:
But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:30

If you were to ask what single discovery made John Bunyan, the answer would be a sentence that fell on his soul one day as he walked in a field near Bedford. He had been through the long storm described in the last chapter. The thunder, he says, had gone beyond him, but some drops still fell; like those who have been scared by fire, he thought every voice cried Fire, fire, and every little touch hurt his tender conscience. And then, suddenly, it was over.

The sentence in the field

“But one day, as I was passing in the field, and that too with some dashes on my conscience, fearing lest yet all was not right, suddenly this sentence fell upon my soul, Thy righteousness is in heaven.” And with it, he says, he seemed to see with the eyes of his soul Jesus Christ at God’s right hand. There, he said to himself, is my righteousness; so that wherever I was, or whatever I was doing, God could not say of me, He wants my righteousness, for that was just before Him.

Then he saw something else, which is the heart of the matter: “it was not my good frame of heart that made my righteousness better, nor yet my bad frame that made my righteousness worse; for my righteousness was Jesus Christ Himself, the same yesterday, and to-day, and for ever.”

Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. HEBREWS 13:8

“Now did my chains fall off my legs indeed,” he writes. He was loosed from his affliction and irons; the dreadful scriptures left off troubling him; he went home rejoicing for the grace and love of God.

Looking in the wrong place

To understand why this set him free, we have to see where he had been looking. For years Bunyan had searched his own heart for his righteousness. He examined his feelings, his faith, his repentance, his thoughts. When his heart was warm, he hoped; when it was cold, he despaired. When a promise comforted him, he was lifted; when a threat struck him, he fell. His peace, he said, would be in and out twenty times a day. He was trying to find in himself the ground of his acceptance with God, and every time he looked he found only sin.

The sentence in the field turned his eyes round. His righteousness was not in his heart at all. It was in heaven, at God’s right hand, in a Person. It did not rise and fall with his frames and feelings, because it was not his frames and feelings. It was Christ.

Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. ROMANS 3:24

This is the doctrine the Reformers called the imputed righteousness of Christ. Bunyan had found it before in Luther’s commentary on Galatians, an old book so worn it was ready to fall to pieces, which, he said, handled his condition as if it had been written out of his own heart; he preferred it, next to the Bible, before all the books he had ever seen, as most fit for a wounded conscience. But there is a difference between reading a doctrine and seeing it. In the field, he saw it.

Gold in the trunk at home

When he got home, he looked for the sentence in his Bible and could not find it, and his heart began to sink. Then 1 Corinthians 1:30 came to mind — Christ is made unto us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption — and he saw that the other sentence was true.

What followed was a season of sweet peace, and he describes it with one of the loveliest images in the book. The graces of God that were now green in him — his faith, his love, his repentance — were, he said, like the cracked groats and fourpence-halfpennies that rich men carry in their purses, when their gold is in their trunks at home. “Oh, I saw my gold was in my trunk at home! In Christ, my Lord and Saviour! Now Christ was all.”

For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God. COLOSSIANS 3:3

One with Christ

Bunyan went further. The Lord led him, he says, into the mystery of union with the Son of God: that he was joined to Him, flesh of His flesh and bone of His bone. If He and I were one, he reasoned, then His righteousness was mine, His merits mine, His victory mine. Now he could see himself in heaven and earth at once — in heaven by his Christ, his head, his righteousness and life, though on earth in his body.

For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones. EPHESIANS 5:30

Why this is the centre of everything

It is not too much to say that the whole of The Pilgrim’s Progress hangs on this sentence. It is why the burden falls at the cross and not at Legality’s house. It is why Christian receives a coat that he did not make, and why he hopes to be known at the gate by that coat. It is why Ignorance, who trusted Christ to make his own obedience acceptable, is turned away. And it is why Christian, sinking in the river and remembering his sins, can still get over: his righteousness was never in the river with him. It was on the other side.

For anxious and scrupulous believers, this is the medicine Bunyan himself needed. The answer to endless self-examination is not a better self-examination. It is to look up. Your frames will change; your feelings will rise and fall; your graces will be green and small. None of that makes your righteousness better or worse, because your righteousness is Jesus Christ Himself.

A caution against misuse

Does this make holiness unimportant? Ignorance thought it would, and Bunyan answered him: true faith in Christ’s righteousness bows the heart to love God, His word, His ways and His people. Bunyan’s own life after the field was one of costly obedience, twelve years in gaol among it. The righteousness in heaven does not make us careless on earth. It makes us free to obey out of gratitude rather than fear. And it does not mean that feelings do not matter; Bunyan’s own feelings in the field were overflowing joy. It means only that feelings are not the foundation.

There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. ROMANS 8:1
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where have you been looking for your righteousness — in your feelings, your performance, your spiritual frames? Name it honestly.

2. Say to yourself several times this week, especially in low moments: my righteousness is in heaven; it is Jesus Christ Himself.

3. Read Philippians 3:7–11 and 1 Corinthians 1:30, and underline every phrase that locates your righteousness in Christ.

4. Think of your own graces as pocket money and Christ as your gold at home. What difference does that make to how you handle failure?

5. If a friend is tormented by self-examination, share Bunyan’s sentence with them, gently, and point them upward.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are my righteousness, at the right hand of God. It is not my good frame that makes it better, nor my bad frame that makes it worse.
Forgive me for searching my own heart for what can only be found in You. Turn my eyes upward.
Let my chains fall off, as Bunyan’s did, and let me go home rejoicing in Your grace.
And since my gold is safe in heaven, make me free and glad to spend my small coins in Your service here. Amen.
