fields.title: The Preacher in Bedford Gaol
fields.body_html:
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body. HEBREWS 13:3

The last pages of Grace Abounding turn from Bunyan’s inner battles to his public calling: how a tinker became a preacher, and how the preacher became a prisoner. They are short, plain and among the most moving things he wrote. They show what the gospel he had discovered looked like when it cost him his liberty.

Called by the church

Bunyan did not appoint himself. Some of the most able among the Bedford congregation, seeing his gift, asked him to speak a word of exhortation to them. It abashed him, but he consented, first twice in private assemblies, then as some of them went into the villages to teach. At last, after solemn prayer and fasting, the church called him to a more public preaching of the word, both to believers and to those who had not yet received the faith. Even then he was, he says, most sorely afflicted with the fiery darts of the devil concerning his own eternal state.

As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. 1 PETER 4:10

It is worth noticing the order. The church recognised the gift, tested it, prayed and sent him. He did not wait until he felt fit; he never did. And the people came by hundreds from all parts to hear the tinker, and some were awakened. At first he could not believe God would speak by him to the heart of any man. Only when they persisted in blessing God for him did he begin to conclude that God had owned in His work such a foolish one as he.

I preached what I felt

Bunyan’s account of his own preaching is famous. For the first two years, he says, he preached chiefly the terror of the law and the guilt of sin, because that was what lay on his own conscience. “I preached what I felt, what I smartingly did feel, even that under which my poor soul did groan and tremble to astonishment.” And then: “I went myself in chains to preach to them in chains; and carried that fire in my own conscience that I persuaded them to beware of.” He would go to the pulpit door full of guilt and terror; it would be lifted while he preached; and before he got down the pulpit stairs it would return.

For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus’ sake. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:5

Later, when God gave him settled peace, he laboured to hold forth Jesus Christ in all His offices and benefits. But the principle stayed the same: he preached what he saw and felt, and there was no gap between the man and the message.

Arrested at Samsell

In November 1660, as we saw in chapter two, Bunyan was taken at a meeting of good people in the country, among whom, he says, had they let him alone, he would have preached that day. He was brought before a justice, who would have released him if his sureties would be bound that he should preach no more. They would not, and he would not. He was indicted for upholding unlawful assemblies and for not conforming to the national worship, sentenced, and sent home to prison, where, writing years later, he says he had lain complete twelve years.

Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men. ACTS 5:29

An inlet into the Word

What was prison like for his soul? Surprisingly, he says it was a time of great content, through grace, though with many turnings upon his heart. And then this: “I never had in all my life so great an inlet into the Word of God as now.” Scriptures in which he had seen nothing before now shone on him. Jesus Christ was never more real and apparent. A handful of passages became especially precious — John 14:1–4, John 16:33, Colossians 3:3–4, Hebrews 12:22–24 — so that at times he could laugh at destruction.

Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. JOHN 14:1–2

The flesh from the bones

But he does not pretend it was easy. The parting with his wife and poor children, he says, was often to him in that place “as the pulling the flesh from the bones.” Above all he grieved for his blind daughter Mary, who lay nearer his heart than all the rest. He imagined her beaten, begging, hungry, cold, and cried, though I cannot now endure the wind should blow upon thee. He saw himself as a man pulling down his house on the heads of his wife and children. “yet thought I, I must do it, I must do it.”

Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive; and let thy widows trust in me. JEREMIAH 49:11

What held him were two texts, of which this was one, and a conviction: if he ventured all for God, he engaged God to take care of his concerns; if he forsook God, he could not expect God to keep them. “I must venture you all with God,” he wrote, “though it goeth to the quick to leave you.”

This is hard teaching, and it must not be twisted. Bunyan did not treat his family lightly; the passage is soaked in anguish. He did not neglect them; he made laces in prison to support them, and Elizabeth pleaded his cause before the judges. And his case was extreme: a direct command to stop preaching Christ. Most of us are never asked to choose so starkly, and Scripture commands us to provide for our own. But where the choice truly comes, Bunyan shows that it is possible to love one’s family deeply and still put Christ first.

Off the ladder blindfold

The last great temptation in Grace Abounding came early in his imprisonment. Not knowing the law, he thought he might be hanged. And Satan asked him: what if, when you come to die, you have no evidence for heaven? At that time, he says, all the things of God were hid from his soul. He feared he would climb the ladder with a pale face and tottering knees and shame the gospel. He prayed for comfort, and none came, for many weeks.

At last one thought fell on him: it was for the word and way of God that he was there, so he must not flinch a hair’s breadth. God might choose whether to comfort him now or at the hour of death; but he might not choose whether to hold his profession. “I was bound, but he was free.” And so he resolved: “I will leap off the ladder even blindfold into eternity, sink or swim, come heaven, come hell, Lord Jesus, if thou wilt catch me, do; if not, I will venture for thy name.”

Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him. JOB 13:15

No sooner had he resolved it than a word dropped on him: Doth Job serve God for nought? He saw at once that to serve God when all is taken away is the very mark of an upright soul. His heart was full of comfort, and he said he would not have been without that trial for much.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Do you preach — in a pulpit, a classroom, a home — what you have felt? Ask God to make your words match your experience of Him.

2. Pray this week for Christians imprisoned for their faith, and for their families.

3. Is there a gift in you that your church has recognised and you have buried out of fear? Talk to your pastor about it.

4. What would you find hardest to venture with God? Bring it to Him in prayer, with Jeremiah 49:11.

5. If comfort has been withheld from you for a long time, consider Bunyan’s resolution: to serve God for nothing, and venture on His name.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You called a tinker to preach and made a prison into a house of Your word. Thank You for Your servant’s faithfulness.
Give me grace to speak what I have felt and seen of You, and to hold my profession whatever it costs.
For those I love, I venture them all with You; preserve them, and let them trust in You.
And when all comfort is hidden, teach me to leap into Your arms blindfold, trusting that You will catch me. Amen.

Is there a gift in you that your church has recognised and you have buried out of fear? Talk to your pastor about it. 4. What would you find hardest to venture with God? fields.title: Christiana and the Weak Pilgrims
fields.body_html:
He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young. ISAIAH 40:11

Some years after the First Part, Bunyan published a Second Part of The Pilgrim’s Progress. It is a different kind of book: gentler, slower, more crowded, more domestic. Christian is gone over the river. Now his wife Christiana, who had hardened her heart against him, repents and sets out after him with her four boys and her young neighbour Mercy. They walk the same road, past the same places, but they travel in company, with a strong guide, and they gather up on the way a remarkable collection of weak, frightened and disabled pilgrims. If the First Part is Bunyan’s book for the struggling soul, the Second Part is his book for the church — and especially for its weakest members.

Christiana’s turning

Christiana’s conversion begins with grief and remorse. After her husband has gone, she remembers his groans and tears, and how she hardened her heart against all his entreaties. It returns upon her like a flash of lightning. Then a messenger named Secret brings her a letter from the King inviting her to come, and she sets out. Her neighbour Mercy comes with her, first only to see her a little way, then for good.

The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. 2 PETER 3:9

For every reader who has prayed long for a husband, a wife or a child, the Second Part is a comfort. Christian ran with his fingers in his ears while his family called him back. Years later, the family came. At the gate, Mercy, who has no letter of invitation, is so afraid of being refused that she faints outside; the keeper takes her by the hand and bids her arise, and lets her in. No one who knocks is turned away.

Great-heart the guide

At the Interpreter’s house Christiana’s company is given a guide: a servant named Great-heart, armed with sword, helmet and shield. He walks before them, answers their questions, explains the places Christian passed, and fights for them — against Giant Grim, Giant Maul, Giant Slay-good and at last Giant Despair himself.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account. HEBREWS 13:17

Great-heart is Bunyan’s portrait of the pastor as protector. He is strong, patient, cheerful and above all careful of the weak. Here, though, the honest caution belongs. The Second Part assumes, as a matter of course, that women travelling need a man to guide and guard them, and some of its remarks about women reflect the assumptions of seventeenth-century England more than anything Scripture requires. Christiana and Mercy are among Bunyan’s most lovely characters — Christiana’s repentance, Mercy’s tender conscience and cheerful industry are drawn with real warmth, and the book honours women’s faith. But readers should enjoy the portrait without treating its social arrangements as a pattern for today. What remains timeless is the picture of a guide who fights for those in his care.

Mr Fearing

The most memorable of the weak pilgrims is one we never meet directly. As the company walks, an old man named Honest asks Great-heart whether he knew Mr Fearing. Great-heart knew him well: he was his guide. Honest sums him up: “He was a man that had the root of the matter in him; but he was one of the most troublesome pilgrims that ever I met with in all my days.”

Great-heart tells his story. Mr Fearing lay roaring at the Slough of Despond for above a month, and would not venture over, though many offered him their hands; yet he would not go back either. At the gate he stood back and let others go in before him, afraid to knock. At the Interpreter’s house he lay in the cold outside for days. He loved those houses but durst not be so bold as to ask. The Hill Difficulty and the lions did not trouble him, for his fear was not about hardship but about his acceptance at the last. In the Valley of Humiliation, strangely, he was better than anywhere else; he would lie down and kiss the very flowers. In the Valley of the Shadow he cried out that the hobgoblins would have him — and Great-heart noticed that the valley was as quiet then as he ever knew it, as if the enemies had a special command not to meddle till Mr Fearing had passed. And at the river, where he feared he would drown, the water was lower than Great-heart had ever seen it, so that he went over not much above wet-shod.

A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench. ISAIAH 42:3

Was he well at last? “Yes, yes,” says Great-heart; “I never had doubt about him.” He was a man of a choice spirit, above many tender of sin, only always kept very low. And then Great-heart explains, in a lovely image, that some must pipe and some must weep; Mr Fearing played upon the bass, whose notes are more doleful than others — but the bass is the ground of music, and God plays upon that string first when He sets the soul in tune for Himself.

Feeble-mind, Ready-to-halt, Despondency and Much-afraid

The company gathers others. Great-heart rescues Mr Feeble-mind from Giant Slay-good. Feeble-mind begs to come behind, lest his many infirmities burden the others; he is offended by what others can bear, and troubled when he hears others rejoice. Great-heart answers that it is his commission to comfort the feeble-minded and support the weak, and that the company will be made all things to him rather than leave him behind. Then Mr Ready-to-halt comes by on crutches, and lends Feeble-mind one of them.

Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:14

When the company comes to By-path Meadow, they go over the stile, kill Giant Despair, and demolish Doubting Castle. In it they find Mr Despondency, almost starved to death, and his daughter Much-afraid. And then comes one of the most joyful scenes in the book. Christiana plays the viol and Mercy the lute, and Ready-to-halt takes Much-afraid by the hand, and they dance in the road. He cannot dance without one crutch in his hand, but, says Bunyan, he footed it well, and the girl answered the music handsomely. Despondency, meanwhile, is for feeding rather than dancing, and Christiana gives him food.

A church for the weak

The Second Part teaches something the First Part could not. A pilgrim does not go alone. The strong carry the weak; the guide adapts his pace; the fearful are given special care; the disabled dance. Bunyan’s church in Bedford was full of poor, unlettered, anxious people, and he loved them. The Second Part is his picture of what a congregation should be: not a company of spiritual athletes, but a household that brings everyone home.

We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves. ROMANS 15:1
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. If you have prayed long for a family member to follow Christ, take heart from Christiana. Write their name and keep praying.

2. Are you a Mr Fearing? Hear Great-heart’s verdict: the root of the matter is in you, and God will make allowances on the road.

3. Who are the Feeble-minds and Ready-to-halts in your church? Choose one to walk beside this month.

4. How could your congregation better welcome people with disabilities, anxieties or weak faith, so that infirmity is no block to their entertainment?

5. Find a reason to rejoice with someone who has come out of Doubting Castle — and if you can, dance.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You gather the lambs in Your arms and gently lead the weak. Thank You for Your patience with fearful pilgrims like me.
For those I love who have not yet come, be longsuffering, and bring them after me as You brought Christiana.
Make me a Great-heart to the feeble and a friend to the disabled; let no infirmity be a block to our welcome.
And bring all Your company home — the strong and the weak, the fearful and the bold — together into Your city. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. HEBREWS 11:13

At the end of the First Part of The Pilgrim’s Progress, Bunyan turns to his reader in a short poem. He has told his dream, he says; now see if you can interpret it, to yourself or to your neighbour. Take heed of misinterpreting it; do not play with the outside of the dream, but look within the veil. It is a fair challenge to put at the end of this book too. We have walked the road with Christian and Hopeful, and with Christiana and her company, and we have listened to Bunyan telling the story of his own soul. What is the dream about?

The road

It is about a road. The Christian life, for Bunyan, is a journey with a beginning and an end. It begins with a burden and a book and a cry: What shall I do to be saved? It passes through a narrow gate that is opened with all the heart to anyone who knocks. It goes by the cross, where the burden falls and is seen no more. And then it goes on — up hills, down into valleys, through a fair where everything is for sale, past castles and counterfeit pilgrims and pleasant meadows that lead off the way — until it comes to a river with no bridge and a city on the other side.

The Person

And it is about a Person. Everything on the road depends on Christ. Goodwill at the gate, the man with the oil behind the wall, the cross and the sepulchre, the Lord of the hill who slew him that had the power of death, the King who opens the gate at last — all are Christ. The sentence that made Bunyan was not about the road at all, but about where his righteousness was: in heaven, at God’s right hand, in Jesus Christ Himself. The road is hard because the world, the flesh and the devil are hard. But it is safe, because He walks it with us and has already arrived at the end.

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. HEBREWS 12:2

What Bunyan offers us

Why should we still read a seventeenth-century tinker? Because he tells the truth about the Christian life. He does not pretend it is easy. His hero falls into bogs, turns aside, sleeps, loses his assurance, is beaten, imprisoned, tempted to despair and to self-destruction, and dies in terror. And yet his hero gets home. There are few more honest books, and few more hopeful.

Because he knew the fearful and the weak. Mr Fearing and Feeble-mind and Much-afraid, the man in the Slough and the man in the valley who hears blasphemies he did not choose, are drawn with a tenderness that only someone who had been there could manage. Many anxious believers have found in Bunyan the first person who seemed to understand them.

Reading him wisely

We have also tried to read him honestly. The Pilgrim’s Progress is an allegory, not Scripture, and not every detail of Christian’s journey will be ours. Bunyan’s own soul-history includes an anxiety so extreme that his readers need to handle it with care, especially those who are tender of conscience; the road out of it, for him and for us, was to look away from self to Christ. His polemics against Rome and his assumptions about women belong to his century. None of these things diminishes him. They make him a real man, and his book a real book, to be read under the Bible and not beside it.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21

Your own dream

The best thing this book can do is send you to Bunyan’s own pages. Read The Pilgrim’s Progress, slowly, both parts. Read Grace Abounding, perhaps with a friend if you are prone to fear. And then read your own life as a pilgrim’s road. Where did your burden fall? Where have you been beaten, imprisoned, rescued? Who was your Evangelist, your Help, your Faithful, your Hopeful, your Great-heart? What key have you found in your bosom? What river is ahead?

Bunyan ends his First Part by looking into the city as the gates close behind Christian and Hopeful, and wishing himself among them. May that be where this book leaves you: not admiring a dream, but longing for the city, and walking towards it.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Draw a simple map of your own pilgrimage so far, marking the places that correspond to Bunyan’s: gate, cross, hill, valley, castle, mountain.

2. Choose one chapter of this book that spoke most directly to you, and act this week on one of its application points.

3. Decide when you will read The Pilgrim’s Progress, or read it again, and with whom.

4. Name one weak pilgrim you could help on the road, and one strong pilgrim you could ask to help you.

5. Spend time thanking God that your righteousness is in heaven, and that He will bring you over the river.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are the way, and You are the end of the way. Thank You for Your servant John Bunyan, who walked the road before me and drew it so that I could see it.
Keep me on the narrow way. Lift me out of every slough, bring me back from every by-path, and set me free from every castle of despair.
Make me a help to weak pilgrims and a faithful companion to strong ones. Let my righteousness be in You alone.
And when I come to the river, let me feel the bottom and find it good, and bring me through the gate into the city, to see Your face. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to John Bunyan
fields.body_html:
Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. PSALM 119:105

Bunyan wrote around sixty works in the thirty-odd years of his ministry — treatises, sermons, controversies, allegories and verse — and all of them are long out of copyright. Most readers need only a handful. Here is a short map.

Begin here

The Pilgrim’s Progress. Begin here, and come back here. Read the First Part through, preferably in an edition that keeps Bunyan’s margin references, since half the meaning is in the Scriptures he cites. Then read the Second Part, which is slower and gentler and repays patience. Both parts are in the Ochorus library. Many readers find it helps to read aloud; Bunyan wrote for the ear.

Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners. His spiritual autobiography, published in 1666, and the key to everything else. It is in the Ochorus library, with the short accounts of his call to preach and his imprisonment. Read it for its honesty about temptation and for the sentence in the field. If you are prone to anxious fears about your salvation, read it with a friend and keep going to the end.

The other allegories

The Holy War. A long allegory of the siege, fall and recapture of the town of Mansoul, contested between Shaddai and Diabolus. It is more elaborate and more military than The Pilgrim’s Progress, and less loved, but full of shrewd observation about the soul.

The Life and Death of Mr Badman. A dialogue tracing the life of a thoroughly bad man from boyhood to a quiet death — Bunyan’s grim counterpart to the pilgrim’s journey, and a sharp portrait of ordinary wickedness in a seventeenth-century town.

Sermons and treatises

Come and Welcome to Jesus Christ. An extended exposition of John 6:37, him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. Perhaps the warmest of all his books, and the best companion to the chapter on the wicket gate.

The Jerusalem Sinner Saved. Written near the end of his life, on Christ’s command that the gospel be preached first at Jerusalem: that the worst sinners are especially invited.

The Heavenly Footman. A short, vigorous sermon on running the race so as to obtain. Good for the sluggish.

Saved by Grace, The Fear of God and The Acceptable Sacrifice are sound, pastoral treatises, plainer than the allegories but full of the same spirit. I Will Pray with the Spirit, written in prison, is his short book on prayer and on the freedom of Spirit-led prayer against set forms.

Approach with care

Bunyan’s controversial writings — against the Quakers early in his ministry, and on baptism and communion later — show him as a vigorous, sometimes harsh debater. They are worth reading for the history, and his case that disagreement over water baptism should not bar believers from fellowship still speaks. But they are not the place to begin. A Few Sighs from Hell, an early sermon on the rich man and Lazarus, is powerful but relentless, and anxious readers may wish to leave it aside.

About Bunyan

John Brown’s John Bunyan: His Life, Times and Work (1885), by a later minister of Bunyan’s own Bedford congregation, remains a full and affectionate life. Christopher Hill’s A Turbulent, Seditious, and Factious People (1988) sets Bunyan in the radical world of the English Revolution; it is learned and illuminating, though its interests are more political than devotional. Richard L. Greaves’s Glimpses of Glory (2002) is the most thorough modern scholarly study. For a warm and readable introduction, Faith Cook’s Fearless Pilgrim (2008) is a good place to start. And the Ochorus biography of Bunyan, on his author page, tells the story briefly.

Counsels for reading him

Read him with the Bible open. His margins are a running concordance; follow them, and you will learn more Scripture than you expected.

Read him as a friend, not a rule. He is describing a road, not setting an examination. Your journey will not match Christian’s in every detail.

Read him for Christ. Bunyan asks his readers, at the close of the First Part, to throw away his dross and keep his gold. The gold is always the same: Christ crucified, Christ our righteousness in heaven, Christ with us in the river.
